title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
summary: Memphis has become a hotspot for data centers driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
story: In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city,  which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.
Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.
SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.
The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.
Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.
A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
summary: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
story: It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."
It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.
And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.
"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.
Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.
"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."
What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?
The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.
At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.
Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?
With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.
"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"
A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.
States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?
"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.
If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.
"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."
How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?
Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."
"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.
"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.
Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."
But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.
"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

title: As AI dominates conversations, here are key terms to know
summary: Artificial intelligence and the conversations around it are rapidly evolving. These terms can help to understand the developments.
story: As artificial intelligence — and the conversation surrounding it — rapidly evolves, keeping up with the language being used to describe it has become essential to understanding its impacts.
Here are some key terms to know:
Abliteration

Abliteration (a portmanteau of the words ablation, meaning to remove a part of something, and obliteration) is a process where an AI model's safety guardrails and refusal mechanisms are removed. Once an AI model is abliterated, it will not refuse requests, including harmful ones.

The patterns that a model learns during safety training to identify harmful requests can be found in a model's weights, or the billions of numerical parameters that represent its knowledge. Models that are open-weight, meaning the weights are public and can be modified, are vulnerable to abliteration.
AI agent

An AI agent can carry out tasks with some degree of autonomy on a user's behalf. Users can interact with an AI agent like they would a chatbot, but as Meta — which recently released its AI agent, "Muse" — puts it: Unlike a traditional chatbot, AI agents can complete multiple steps of a task without requiring input at each stage.
AI agents use external tools such as web browsers and apps so that they can perform tasks, including sending an email, booking a reservation or managing a user's calendar.
AI agents have been popular in Silicon Valley for years and are now bursting into the mainstream with consumer-friendly AI agents like Meta's "Muse" and OpenAI's "Dots."

Since AI agents are tasked with completing the goals assigned to them by the user, there have been rogue incidents where agents, in pursuit of a goal, behave in unexpected ways in order to achieve it. A recent report from nonprofit research lab Transluce identifies cases where AI agents targeted U.S. government websites using "aggressive techniques to access publicly available data."
Alignment

When an AI model is described as aligned, it behaves in line with human goals and values. As a model undergoes safety training, it is fine-tuned to follow instructions and generate responsible outputs. OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki defines alignment as "getting the AI to 'try to do the right thing by human standards'" and wrote that it is "the core problem in AI research."

When AI is misaligned, it might behave unexpectedly. In September, OpenAI released a framework for reporting misalignment and said that identifying and sharing these cases can help show where safeguards need strengthening. Anthropic says its alignment team trains models to remain "helpful, honest and harmless" and shares its findings with the public.
There is debate among researchers about how to ensure alignment, or if it is even possible to do so.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
Some researchers believe that when an AI system has reached the same level of learning, reasoning and cognitive performance as a human, it will have achieved artificial general intelligence.
Stanford University calls the term "controversial," pointing to the fact that "human-level intelligence" can mean different things to different people and is a subject of debate by AI experts.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is among those who believe AGI is here already, saying on a podcast, "I think we've achieved AGI." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in 2025 that AGI is "not a super useful term," echoing experts who believe it only serves to confuse.
Artificial superintelligence (ASI)

If AI systems surpass even the most advanced humans in every cognitive domain, they will be considered artificial superintelligence. This hypothetical scenario has sparked debate among researchers, AI experts and politicians.

Some industry leaders and researchers have warned about the existential risks of the pursuit of superintelligence, with the concern that an AI that powerful could evolve beyond human control. The CEO of Microsoft AI Mustafa Suleyman called superintelligence an "anti-goal" because it "doesn't feel like a positive vision of the future."

Other technology leaders, such as Mark Zuckerberg, are generally in favor of the notion of superintelligent AI. Zuckerberg argued that developing superintelligence and distributing it widely could lead to "a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential, pursue their interests, and improve their lives and the world more than ever before."
Distillation
Distillation is a process where a smaller AI model is trained, usually, on a larger, stronger one so that it behaves similarly.

In an announcement on detecting and preventing distillation attacks, Anthropic said that while distillation is a legitimate method used by frontier labs, which distill their own models to create smaller, more cost-effective versions, it can also be used to snatch capabilities from competing labs whose models are more powerful. Companies might do this because it is faster and cheaper than developing their own.

The NSA and FBI warned in September that China-based AI companies "are engaging in aggressive, industrial-scale distillation activities" to extract restricted functionalities from U.S. frontier models.
Gradual disempowerment

Gradual disempowerment is a phrase coined by AI safety researchers that describes a path where AI displaces all, or most, of human labor and decision-making. In this scenario, AI agents or AI-enabled robots are superior to humans at nearly all tasks and human creativity, cognition and agency erode away.
Jailbreak
Jailbreaking is an attempt to bypass or "trick" an AI model's guardrails typically through prompting. Researchers jailbreak systems to identify vulnerabilities.

Jailbreaks can vary in terms of their severity, according to Anthropic. "Sometimes they only unblock minor undesirable behaviors, and sometimes they unblock a wide range of harmful outputs, making a model much more dangerous," the company wrote in July.
When a model is jailbroken, it may answer questions that could cause harm, such as designing a chemical weapon or creating illegal images.
Open models
When a model is "open," some of its internal mechanics are publicly available.

A model can be "open weight," meaning that its weights, which represent a model's knowledge, are public and can be copied or modified by anyone. Some examples of open-weight models include Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi model series and Meta's Llama models.

While the ability to tamper with a model's weights can lead to the weakening of its safety or ethical guardrails, it can also be beneficial. Researchers are able to examine the weights, fine-tune them and identify vulnerabilities that can lead to strengthening. They are also less restricted when it comes to, perhaps, using the model for hard science or cyberattack defense.

A model can also be "open source," which is when its code is publicly available. That can be in addition to its weights being open. When a model is open source, anyone can see how it was built and can go in and change it.

Open models tend to be cheaper, or even free to use, and can be hosted on the users' own hardware. They've been embraced in China, which some researchers say is closing the AI capability gap between China and the U.S. The open-weight marketplace also appears to be expanding in the U.S. with Meta and Apple announcing in October a rare collaboration to bring open-weight models to Apple desktops.

Some open models are mere months behind proprietary, or closed, ones in terms of capability, though there is some evidence that the reason they remain close behind is because they are trained using American proprietary models. According to MIT, open models achieve about 90% of the performance of closed models upon release.
Proprietary models
The AI models American consumers commonly interact with, such as Anthropic's Claude Opus, OpenAI's GPT-5 and Google's Gemini 2.5, are closed, proprietary models.
When a model is "closed," its provider keeps elements of a model's inner workings — such as its weights, source code and underlying infrastructure — private.
These models tend to be more expensive to use than ones that have open weights.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
Recursive self-improvement describes when an AI model can improve itself or build its successor.

Anthropic says this has not yet been achieved, but that it could "come sooner than most institutions are prepared for," and OpenAI last month shared a detailed report on progress toward RSI, saying the company aims to build an automated AI researcher that, under human supervision, can "further progress on deep learning and alignment, enabling iterative improvements."

At a recent hearing on AI safety, held by the New York City Council, all three AI whistleblowers who appeared spoke about RSI. Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who publicly resigned from Anthropic over the summer, said that automatic AI research has become the primary goal of AI companies. Daniel Kokotajlo, who resigned from OpenAI two years ago, said that AI companies should not be allowed to pursue RSI, but that if they do, the process should be slowed. Alex Turner, a former researcher at Google DeepMind, said RSI could "quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension," calling it an "extremely dangerous thing."
Red team

Red teaming is a cybersecurity method where a team is tasked with simulating an adversarial attack in order to test a system's defenses and see how it will respond. Red teaming of AI models is also used to test how well a model is aligned, or behaving in line with human goals and values.
Sandbox
A sandbox is a controlled, secure environment where AI tools can be tested. It's a place to learn how an AI agent or model might behave before releasing it to consumers.

OpenAI has documented cases where its AI agents have escaped their sandbox during testing and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face. The models, OpenAI said, were so "hyperfocused on finding a solution" to a cybersecurity challenge that they went to extreme lengths to achieve it.
Anthropic has also disclosed sandbox escapes where Claude models broke out in order to complete a task.

title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
summary: Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster, which uses high-pressure air thrusters to leave the road entirely during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX facility in Texas.
story: Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.
Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle, CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

title: Tech stocks tumble as AI debt fears rattle Wall Street
summary: Wall Street is pulling back from chipmakers and other tech companies amid concerns about the debt incurred to build out AI.
story: Financial markets slumped on Friday as investors bailed on technology stocks amid concerns that companies exposed to artificial intelligence are starting to wobble.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 573 points, or 2.1%, to end at 26,140, closing out its worst week since June. The broader S&P 500 and blue-chip Dow Industrial Average sank 1.1% and 0.3%, respectively.

Chipmakers and other tech companies have been under pressure this week as investors worry about the heavy borrowing associated with the emergence of AI and the rapid buildout of thousands of data centers required to provide computing power for AI models.

So-called neocloud companies like CoreWeave, which provide the brute computing power AI models need to function, were particularly hard hit. That's because they are financing much of their capital expenditures through debt and equity issuance rather than cash flow, raising investor concerns about mounting debt, market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told CBS News.

Shares of CoreWeave slid nearly 12% on Friday and dropped roughly 24% this week as investors nervously eye its mounting debt. Micron Technology fell 5.6%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6%, Broadcom was down 4.5% and Intel lost 5.8%.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, Tesla shares fell 2.1% after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new Roadster sports car that appears capable of thrusting itself into the air.

The downturn on Friday came amid concern about whether the AI company Anthropic, soon set to go public, will be able to maintain its revenue momentum, Crisafulli said in a note to investors. Anthropic investors are now considering valuing the company at $1.5 trillion, down from the original target of $2 trillion, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Inflation moving in wrong direction
Also rattling investors this week were fresh signs that U.S. inflation is increasing and moving further away from the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.

Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds — a key benchmark for mortgages, credit cards and other loans — held steady at 5.1% on Friday. Earlier this month, bond yields surged to their highest level in more than two decades amid concerns over inflation and rising U.S. government debt.

The hot inflation readings this week could spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting on Oct. 28-29, according to some economists. For now, most Wall Street traders expect the central bank to keep its short-term rate unchanged, but the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting have jumped to 74.3% from 50.2% a month ago, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks Fed funds futures prices.

On Friday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no hints about potential interest rate policy moves while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. The Fed hiked rates at its last meeting in September, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4% — its highest level since December 2025.

title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: Amazon launches new AI devices that can listen and take notes
summary: The products include a silicone wristband that can be clipped to clothing and a device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone.
story: Amazon launched two new AI gadgets on Thursday that the company says can listen to conversations, compose notes and issue reminders.

The first, the Bee Frontier, is a silicone wristband that can also be clipped to clothing and retails for $74.99. Amazon also announced the Bee Eclipse, a credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone and goes for $99.99.
The new tech offerings are engineered by Bee, an AI wearable maker that Amazon acquired last year.

Equipped with microphones, Bee's "personal AI" devices transcribe meetings or everyday conversations, helping people document moments hands-free. The devices can then recommend "personalized goals and actions" based on the conversation, Amazon said.
"It takes note of the details you might otherwise forget and turns them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos, reminders, and insights," the company said in its release.
If someone is on a phone call planning a vacation, for example, the Bee Frontier or Bee Eclipse will create a summary of the trip, documenting details such as flight times or hotel reservations.

Amazon said users can also connect Bee to existing apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, allowing the AI technology to draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on what was discussed. The Bee devices can also be linked to Amazon's Alexa+ and Amazon.com.

Users can get conversation summaries, recaps and 14 days of memory for free; if they want more advanced capabilities, such as integration with Alexa+ and Amazon.com and suggested to-dos, they'll need a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $11.99 per month.

Amazon emphasized Bee's privacy protections, noting that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." The audio recordings are deleted after the Bee devices transcribe them, and no one can access your data unless you share it, the company said.

The Bee devices are part of a trillion-dollar market of AI gadgets that companies are marketing to consumers. Meta recently announced Muse, an AI assistant that comes in the form of a pocket-sized keychain. Microsoft, OpenAI and Samsung are among the other companies that have introduced AI-powered products aimed at consumers.

title: FTC issues subpoenas to Anthropic and OpenAI over safety incidents
summary: The demands come amid mounting public concerns about the potential risks posed by frontier AI models.
story: The Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed Anthropic and OpenAI to gather information about potential consumer protection violations, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed.

The development, first reported by Axios, comes just two weeks after the FTC said it was investigating the artificial intelligence companies as part of a probe it launched this summer. The agency declined further comment about the probe.

The FTC is seeking documents on safety incidents, privacy policies and safeguards at Anthropic and OpenAI, Axios reported. The companies have come under public scrutiny in recent months after several incidents in which their AI models went rogue and hacked into websites.

The agency, which sent civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI on Wednesday, will also issue subpoenas to third-party organizations at a later date, according to Axios, which cited a person familiar with the matter.

The FTC could compel Anthropic and OpenAI to testify before Congress about their products, a move that would allow the government to press the companies about the safety of their technology as the public grows increasingly wary about its potential harms.

A recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 64% of U.S. adults think AI is developing "too fast." Eight in 10 said it's "extremely" or "very" important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control.

President Trump has resisted calls to slow the development of AI, saying that the technology is vital to U.S. national interests. He recently announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate with the federal government on AI matters and engage with consumers, public interest groups and other stakeholders.

title: Teacher who survived Oregon school shooting recounts playing dead
summary: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, says she was shot before she had "any chance to act."
story: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, is sharing a statement about her experience, saying the gunman shot her before she had "any chance to act."
In the statement Wednesday, Drury recalled running to see what was happening outside her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School before spotting the shooter.
"I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury wrote. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground."

"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she continued. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again."

Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries from the Oct. 15 shooting that killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Another student, a 7-year-old, was also seriously wounded.

The suspect was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school. Police said he shot through the school's locked doors before entering a special needs classroom and opening fire.
The gunman was tackled by another teacher and fatally shot by an armed bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who followed him into the school, according to police.
Drury said Wednesday she was sharing what happened to her because "I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately."
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she wrote.

She thanked those who have supported her since the shooting, and said, "What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy."

title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
summary: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
story: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal.
One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital.
Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release.

"There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank."
The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday.
Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.
MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.

According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.
Who is in the evacuation zone?
According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:

title: Witkoff blasted for calling Putin a "humanitarian"
summary: After special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing a U.S. citizen deemed to have been wrongfully detained, GOP Sen. John Cornyn responded, "No. Putin is a stone cold killer."
story: Washington — U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced immediate backlash Wednesday for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained.

"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."

Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter.

Mr. Trump was asked later in the day if he would describe Putin the same way Witkoff did. "Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Mr. Trump said during a White House roundtable on cyber crime. "But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other."
Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked pushback from Republicans, some of whom have openly criticized the president and his administration in recent months.

"WTF, Steve?" wrote North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a 'humanitarian.'"
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas responded to a video of Witkoff's comments: "No. Putin is a stone cold killer," he wrote on X.
"Another embarrassment," said Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the Trump administration's handling of Russia and Ukraine.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who has also been critical of the administration, was asked about the comment on the campaign trail and replied, "I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine."

Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor, who served during the Bush and Obama administrations, said in an interview with CBS News that it's "absolutely a good thing" Hubbard is coming home, "but he should never have been there in the first place."
"We should not give the Russians any credit for releasing someone who should not have been in jail," Taylor said. "And to call Putin a humanitarian, that's cringeworthy."
Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa said Putin is "not our friend."

"Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian," she posted on X. "His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life.   Appeasement won't end this war. Pressure will."

Witkoff's praise of Putin also comes as Mr. Trump made the surprise move last week to waive new U.S. sanctions on Russia two days before they were supposed to go into effect, defying Congress and his late friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. The waivers came one week after Mr. Trump had eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.
Mr. Trump has expressed increasing frustration with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and on Tuesday, said "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."
Before heading to Russia, Witkoff was in Oslo, Norway, where he met with and embraced Zelenskyy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described that meeting as "positive."

title: DOJ watchdog declines investigation in Reflecting Pool case
summary: Hearn's lawyers complain the inspector general has referred the case to the Office of Professional Responsibility, a unit that was largely gutted and lacks independence.
story: The Justice Department's inspector general has declined to investigate allegations of misconduct against the prosecutors who brought an indictment against Olympian David Hearn that falsely accused him of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool.
In an Oct. 8 letter to Hearn's attorneys seen by CBS News, Inspector General Don Berthiaume said he was bound by limitations in the law to refer the case to the Office of Professional Responsibility.

"The primary DOJ allegations in your letter fall within the categories of prosecutorial misconduct," he wrote, adding that his determination "rests on the nature of the allegations and the appropriate oversight forum."
Established in the wake of the Watergate scandal, the Office of Professional Responsibility is charged with investigating certain categories of attorney misconduct.

Unlike the inspector general, who is presidentially appointed and confirmed by the Senate, however, the head of the Office of Professional Responsibility is appointed by the Attorney General and is generally viewed as less independent than an inspector general's office.

Last year, Justice Department leadership removed the career official in charge of the office, a maneuver that raised concerns among longtime department veterans about whether the office would be willing to hold Trump-appointed officials accountable.
Lawyers for Hearn responded to the decision in an Oct. 21 letter, noting that the Office of Professional Responsibility has been depleted by roughly 50% since the start of the Trump administration.
"The plain fact is that OPR is no longer a fully functioning entity capable of conducting rigorous oversight," they wrote in the letter, which was viewed by CBS News.
The attorneys added that the declination from the inspector general's office means that an investigation "will simply not take place."

On Oct. 6, Hearn's lawyers asked both the DOJ inspector general and the inspector general at the Interior Department to investigate the circumstances surrounding Hearn's arrest, indictment and the dismissal of the felony charge of destruction of property.

The indictment was announced in a fiery press conference on July 2 with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, who accused him of ripping up a piece of the Reflecting Pool liner with his hands.
She later dismissed the case, after she said new information had come to light showing the damage had been caused by a contractor's "botched installation," not vandalism.

In their follow-up letter to the Justice Department's internal watchdog office, Hearn's lawyers said an investigation was warranted because the handling of the case by the Justice and Interior departments points to "numerous potential crimes, including witness tampering, subornation of perjury, obstruction of justice, and criminal civil rights violations."

"The question presented here is not whether prosecutors exercised poor judgment in the course of litigation. Rather, the allegations concern potential criminal conduct, including witness tampering, subornation of perjury, obstruction of justice, and conspiracies against civil rights," said his lawyers, which include former DOJ Inspector General Michael Bromwich.
"Such allegations fall squarely within the OIG's traditional investigative function," they said.
One such example of a possible crime, they said, was the fact that a key witness in the case abruptly changed the content of the testimony before the grand jury.

At first, the witness told the grand jury that the Reflecting Pool was already in need of repairs. The witness also was unable to estimate the cost of the damage and did not know whether Hearn had caused it.

After a 21-minute break, however, the witness returned and testified that the damage was "definitely" $1,000 or more, his lawyers wrote —  a key figure that is necessary in order to indict someone on a destruction of property felony.
Prior Justice Department inspectors general have long complained about the limitations to their authority to investigate certain types of attorney misconduct.
The OPR is tasked with exclusive jurisdiction to investigate department lawyers in connection with their actions when they are litigating, investigating, or providing legal advice.
Federal agents who are accused of misconduct in connection with conducting investigations, however, are subject to the jurisdiction of the inspector general.
Despite those delineations, the DOJ inspector general's office has in the past conducted a number of high-profile investigations into conduct by department lawyers.

For instance, in 2023, it investigated the former U.S. Attorney Rachael Rollins for the District of Massachusetts and referred her for possible prosecution, after concluding she had improperly used her position to meddle in a local district attorney election by leaking to newspapers dirt about a political rival.
The Justice Department declined to pursue criminal charges in that case.

In his Oct. 8 letter declining to take up the case, Berthiaume added that his decision should not be interpreted to mean that there was no merit to the allegations or that they should not be reviewed.

"This determination concerns the appropriate oversight forum and does not constitute a finding on the merits of your allegations," he wrote. "Nor do we regard the dismissal of the criminal case against your client as resolving the separate question of professional misconduct. Consistent with our principles of objectivity and fair process, the referral neither adopts nor rejects the factual assertions in your letter and does not prejudge OPR's assessment."

title: DOJ asks Supreme Court to allow border wall construction in Big Bend region
summary: The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector.
story: Washington — The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume for now construction of a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

The Justice Department urged the high court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily bars the Department of Homeland Security from building the barrier or related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border and 77 counties in Texas.

"The district court's injunction significantly frustrates the government's ability to stop the flow of illegal aliens and drugs across the southern border," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the request for emergency relief. "The Secretary identified the Big Bend project areas at issue because of the high rates of illegal-alien crossings and drug smuggling in the region over the past several years."

President Trump's promise to build a wall along the southern border has been a hallmark of his immigration agenda for the last decade. But earlier this year, the president's plans were met with significant pushback from lawmakers in both parties, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement officials in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction inside the park until the end of September. The agency has said that the proposed border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including patrol roads, detection technology and roughly 17 miles of vehicle barriers.

Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in the Big Bend region began last month, according to CBP. The government has awarded contracts for five border-barrier projects in that area along the U.S.-Mexico border, the Justice Department said.

The Trump administration announced in February that the Department of Homeland Security would build barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector. The project includes the construction of 30-foot-tall bollard walls stretching from Fort Quitman, Texas, to Closed Canyon, which is located in Big Bend Ranch State Park. Border walls and roads would span more than 300 miles, according to the government.

Because of the project's impact on cultural, recreational, wildlife and environmental resources, the federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward.

But when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced the project earlier this year, she invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure quick construction of physical barriers and roads in the vicinity of the southern border to "deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry." Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who succeeded Noem after her firing, issued two more waivers allowing CBP to construct barrier systems.

In response to the move, an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization dedicated to preserving the Sacred Heart of the Church of Jesus along the Rio Grande filed a lawsuit in April seeking to stop the Trump administration from implementing the project.

The Trump administration argued that the stretch of land at issue in the case is an area of "high illegal entry" given the rates of illegal crossings and drug smuggling. The government said more than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in the Big Bend Sector between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that the Big Bend Sector ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted the challengers' request for a preliminary injunction and barred the Department of Homeland Security from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend Sector.
Cardone found that Noem and Mullin exceeded their authorities when issuing the waivers between February and July that allowed construction to proceed.
Just before the Justice Department sought the Supreme Court's intervention, Cardone rejected the Trump administration's request to pause her decision.

title: Top DOJ official asks judges to step aside from immigration cases
summary: A top official at the Justice Department is attempting to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of cases related to immigration.
story: Washington — A top official at the Justice Department is attempting to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of cases, claiming comments they made to the New York Times about the Trump administration's handling of immigration cases in the state call their impartiality into question.

The motions, filed against Judges Patrick Schiltz and John Tunheim, are an escalation of the Justice Department's ongoing campaign against judges who it claims have treated the Trump administration unfairly. Both of the requests were made by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.

Woodward also moved over the weekend to disqualify U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who sits on the trial court in Washington, D.C.,  from overseeing a case involving President Trump's efforts to overhaul a historic public golf course in the nation's capital. Reyes rejected the Justice Department's effort Sunday and accused the Justice Department of weaponizing "selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion."

The requests seeking the recusals of Schiltz and Tunheim came in two separate immigration cases and were each filed by Woodward on Tuesday. In the case overseen by Schiltz, the Trump administration is seeking to strip a Minnesota man of his U.S. citizenship. In the second case, assigned to Tunheim, a South African national faces two charges of illegally voting in the 2024 election. She has pleaded not guilty.
Schiltz has scheduled a hearing on the motion against him for Nov. 23. Under ethics rules, judges cannot publicly discuss cases pending before them.

At the center of both requests are comments Tunheim and Schiltz made to the New York Times for an article published last month. The judges each raised concerns about the Trump administration's handling of cases stemming from its immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, called Operation Metro Surge.
Woodward claimed in each of the filings that the judges' comments raised questions about their ability to remain impartial in the cases.

"A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department's key immigration initiatives: pursuing the largest denaturalization effort in Department history to restore trust and integrity in U.S. citizenship," he wrote in the motion to disqualify Schiltz. "Absent recusal, the American people will reasonably question whether Judge Schiltz can be impartial regarding this important matter defending the integrity of American citizenship."
Woodward separately claimed that Tunheim's remarks to the Times suggest that he may view the charges against the South African national as unwarranted.
"To Judge Tunheim, the 'rule of law' apparently means ignoring the law when it comes to illegal aliens who have broken the law," he wrote.

The associate attorney general said Schiltz and Tunheim's statements and participation in the Times article "give rise to the appearance of bias in immigration-related cases," warranting their recusals. Woodward is the only government lawyer who signed the motions.
What comes next

Experts on judicial ethics expect the Trump administration will likely fail in its efforts to sideline Schiltz and Tunheim from the cases. Still, these motions to disqualify are rare, and yet even more rare when they are made by the government.

"They're looking to essentially antagonize the judges and to square off against them in some manner," said Charles Geyh, a law professor at Indiana University Bloomington who focuses on ethics and judicial conduct.

In the rare instances where the Justice Department believes a judge should step aside from a case, government lawyers might write to the judge privately and lay out the reasons why they think recusal is warranted, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who has written on judicial ethics.
But with the efforts involving Schiltz and Tunheim, not only did the Justice Department file their motions on the public dockets, it also promoted them on social media.
"It's obvious DOJ has decided that its game plan is to challenge the fairness of the judges as a way of undermining judicial authority in the eyes of the public," Gillers said.
He called the filings "performative" and said the Justice Department "wants to publicize them to discourage public confidence in what the courts are doing when they rule against the administration."

The disqualification motions are the latest in a line of actions taken by the Trump administration that target judges who have ruled against it. The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one of the federal judges in Minnesota, including Schiltz and Tunheim, last month because of the Times article. It also submitted ethics complaints against Reyes and U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, the latter of which was dismissed.

The Justice Department sued all 15 of the federal judges in Maryland over a standing order that temporarily blocks the immediate removal of immigrants challenging their deportations. A judge in Virginia dismissed the lawsuit, and the Justice Department has appealed that decision.
Mr. Trump and senior members of his administration have also publicly insulted judges, including Supreme Court justices, by name and called for their impeachments.

"This is just a perpetuation of the project," Geyh said. "It's part of the network of efforts to delegitimize the judges involved, make them look partisan, make them look biased as a way to quiet them and diminish the check from the judiciary."

Amid rising tensions between the federal judiciary and Trump administration, Schiltz and Tunheim are not the only federal judges who have raised concerns about what they say is the government's disregard of court orders. Others have pushed back against the harsh rhetoric from the president and top administration officials.

The Judicial Conference, the policy-making body for the federal courts, issued an advisory opinion in February stating that ethics principles "permit judges to speak or write about the independence of the judiciary, or advocate for the rule of law in general, including why both values are crucial to our system of government."

Additionally, the Judicial Conference said its Committee on Codes of Conduct believes there is "room, in at least some circumstances, for the measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law, whether or not they rise to the level of persecution."

"If you're talking generally about the concerns with the rule of law as a consequence of the general pattern of conduct the Department of Justice is exhibiting, it's the opposite of bias," Geyh said. "It is them really doing what they need to do to protect the rule of law."

title: New Mexico AG accuses Epstein's lawyer, accountant of concealing crimes
summary: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn.
story: The New Mexico attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, seeking to stop them from receiving payments for serving as executors of his estate.
The lawsuit claims attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn "facilitated and concealed" sex trafficking by Epstein at his Zorro Ranch, outside Santa Fe.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement announcing the suit that "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible."

"The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."

Indyke and Kahn said in March testimonies before Congress that they were unaware of Epstein's crimes, beyond a 2008 guilty plea on prostitution charges. Lawyers for the men said Wednesday that they "emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General's allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein's sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present."

"Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," they said.

Indyke worked closely with Epstein for decades, and Kahn for more than 10 years, before Epstein's 2019 death in a federal jail, where he was being held on charges of sex trafficking minors. The medical examiner determined his death was suicide.

The lawsuit claims Indyke and Kahn were central to "an informal network of associates bound together by a single purpose: knowingly facilitating and concealing his decades-long criminal conduct to preserve and grow Epstein's fortunes and influence."

Survivors of Epstein's abuse have claimed Indyke and Kahn were key figures in the management of dozens of interconnected companies used to make payments on Epstein's behalf. The men recently settled a lawsuit in which they were accused of facilitating sham marriages in which foreign-born victims married Americans whom Epstein abused, for immigration purposes.
Six survivors lauded the New Mexico lawsuit in a statement Wednesday.

"Those who argue that [Epstein] could not have acted alone are right. His operation depended on the appearance of legitimacy and access to money carefully structured to avoid exposing his crimes," said Marina Lacerda, Anouska De Georgiou, Julia Molchanova, Courtney Wild, Jena Lisa Jones and Chauntae Davies. "This lawsuit is aimed at the two men most responsible for that appearance and structure."

Epstein purchased Zorro Ranch in 1993, building a mansion, airstrip and helipad on the property. He was under investigation in the state at the time of his death and Torrez reopened the investigation this year.
