title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in data privacy ruling
summary: A jury found that the social media company had deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.
story: Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.

Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.

In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.

The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled.
"These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.

The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads.
In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."
He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences."
C.J. Mahoney, Meta's Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement that the company is confident it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Where the $25 billion could go
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.
In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.
Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.
Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

title: Childcare costs are growing faster than rent in the U.S.
summary: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.
story: The rising cost of childcare in the U.S. is vying with food prices and healthcare expenses in straining household budgets.

Nearly 8% of families are spending more than $2,000 per month on childcare services, including daycare, nanny services and other programs. That's more than double the share of households that spent that much just three years ago, according to new research from the Bank of America Institute.

In September, the cost of daycare and school-related fees rose faster than other essential expenses, such as rent and medical care, compared to the same period a year ago, according to federal labor data.

Families nationwide spent an average of 8% of their monthly incomes on childcare services in September, BofA found. Under federal guidelines, childcare is considered affordable when it consumes no more than 7% of household income.

Assuming a family spends $24,000 annually on childcare, it would need to earn roughly $343,000 to remain below the 7% threshold. In 2025, median household income was $87,460, according to Census Bureau data.
Lower- and middle-income families spend nearly 9% of their annual incomes on childcare payments, while higher-income households spend 7.3%, according to BofA.

Along with facing rising childcare costs, workers have also seen slowing wage growth, heightening the financial pressure on many families, Economic Policy Institute economist Elise Gould told CBS News.
Separate research from AARP shows that families are turning to grandparents, who provide $172 billion per year in direct financial assistance.
Where are childcare costs growing fastest?

In some parts of the U.S., childcare fees are rising even faster, according to BofA. In September, median childcare costs rose fastest in Nashville, Tennessee, followed by Jacksonville, Florida, and Phoenix, Arizona, compared to the same period a year ago, according to BofA's analysis.

"There's been an increase in domestic migration to these areas," BofA Institute economist Taylor Bowley told CBS News, noting that an increase in demand for childcare services is putting pressure on prices.

A shortage of childcare workers also appears to be driving up childcare expenses. Employment in the sector fell 0.7% in September compared to one year earlier, making it harder for providers to deliver such services.
"You see job growth falling and price pressures creeping in, leading to a bit of an availability problem," BofA Institute senior economist David Tinsley told CBS News.

A lack of affordable childcare disproportionately affects women's employment opportunities, according to the researchers. Women are more likely than men to take on childcare responsibilities, according to data from the American Time Use Survey.
"Beyond childcare being a household expense, it's a form of economic enablement," Bowley said.

title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
summary: Armed and in uniform, agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors to ask residents about their immigration status whether they're registered to vote.
story: Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.
Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."
Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."
One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Hours after this article was published, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand the that DHS immediately cease "law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway." He said the DHS operations "reflect an anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department, and serve only President Trump's voter suppression agenda, not a legitimate enforcement objective."
For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.
"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that —  because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."
"Target List"
In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.
DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally,"  said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."
"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

title: Electricity bills force 1 in 5 to cut back on food, survey finds
summary: Americans living on a fixed income are particularly vulnerable when electricity costs surge, a Consumer Reports expert says.
story: About one in five Americans say they have had to cut back on groceries to afford their electricity bills, while roughly a quarter of consumers are turning down their heating or air conditioning to uncomfortable levels to lower their energy costs, according to a new survey from Consumer Reports.

About 80% of people who have lived in the same home for at least three years say their electricity bills have increased over that time, according to a national survey of more than 2,000 adults by the nonprofit advocacy group. The largest share, 28%, said their bills had surged between 20% and 49% over that period.
Electricity prices across major U.S. cities have jumped 14% over the last three years, according to federal data.

Rising utility costs are worsening the affordability crunch facing millions of American families, who are facing sharply higher gasoline and diesel prices amid higher oil costs due to the war in Iran. The survey found that consumers are cutting back where they can, such as switching to less expensive foods or spending less on discretionary items, to cope with rising electricity bills.

"We're hearing a lot of folks who don't know what they can possibly do to afford rising [electricity] rates," Sara Enright, senior director of safety and energy at Consumer Reports, told CBS News. "Vulnerable populations like students and retirees who live on a fixed income don't have a lot of flex in their budgets, and so when they get a surprise bill in the heat of the summer, it can be frightening."
Consumers often prioritize paying their utility bills because they need to keep their lights on and their refrigerators running, she added.
"People are cutting back on food" to pay their utility bills, Enright said. "They're definitely cutting back on non-essentials like vacations and eating out."

Other polls show that energy costs are weighing on voters ahead of next month's midterm elections, along with other cost-of-living issues. The cost of food is the top concern for voters in battleground states, followed by gas prices and utility bills, according to an October survey from Climate Power, a clean energy advocacy group.
"Increasingly distrustful"

Consumer Reports found that Americans blame their higher electric bills on utility companies seeking to maximize profits and on the rapid buildout of data centers. Electricity demand is forecast to increase 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers across the U.S., according to energy management company Schneider Electric.

The price of natural gas, ongoing electrification of buildings and vehicles, and other factors are also contributing to rising power costs. Meanwhile, a majority of respondents said they don't believe state utility regulators are protecting their interests, Consumer Reports found.

"The public is becoming increasingly distrustful that government is looking out for them, and this is true across party lines," Enright told CBS News. "Everyday people, as the cost of living is rising, are concerned that their needs and interests are not being centered by the politicians and legislators that are supposed to represent them."

As electricity prices spike, more middle-income households are applying for government energy assistance despite their incomes being too high to qualify, Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, told CBS News. The federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program is limited to people who earn less than 60% of their state's median income.

"People are dealing with high food bills, high gasoline bills, and they've just gone through high summer cooling bills," he said. "If you're living on a tight budget, from paycheck to paycheck, then the cost of driving goes up by $100, $150 a month, that might be the whole surplus in your budget."
Consumers "feel the government's not standing behind them, and they can't control these prices," Wolfe added.
Help decoding your energy bill

Consumer Reports said it's launching a new initiative called Power Smarter to help households reduce their energy costs. The effort includes a service called the CR Bill Decoder, where consumers can submit their electric bills. Consumer Reports, which will anonymize the bill data, will use the information to analyze trends and map prices across the U.S.

Bill Decoder "is intended to be a simple first step for anybody who wants to learn more about their energy bill and how they can take more power over their bill," Enright said. "We anonymize it and aggregate the data that we collect from it, and we'll be doing national-level and state-level evaluations of what's driving energy costs, and using that information to advocate for the American consumer to keep energy costs affordable."

title: Supreme Court rejects bid to restrict treatments for trans inmates
summary: In an unsigned order, the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal seeking to revive a policy ending certain medical treatments for transgender inmates.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Wednesday left intact a lower court decision that blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new Bureau of Prisons policy that would end certain medical interventions for transgender inmates.

In an unsigned, one-line order, the high court rejected an emergency appeal from the Justice Department asking it to freeze the district court order and revive the new rules. The policy would cut off surgical and hormone therapy treatments, as well as social accommodations, for inmates who have been or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria.
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas said they would have allowed the Trump administration to enforce the change.
The Trump administration sought the Supreme Court's intervention in the dispute last month and argued that the new policy for transgender inmates is needed to "maintain institutional security."

But lawyers for a transgender woman and two transgender men in federal prisons who challenged the rules said the Bureau of Prisons has provided hormone treatment to people with gender dysphoria since 1992. They said that the new policy required the end of treatment for nearly 1,000 inmates in the bureau's custody.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the inmates, said the Supreme Court's decision is critical for transgender people who are incarcerated in the federal system.

"The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights," Nowlin-Sohl said in a statement. "We will continue to defend the rights of our clients and all incarcerated people."
Case followed Trump executive order

The dispute before the Supreme Court stems from a lawsuit the inmates filed against the Trump administration last year on behalf of incarcerated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. The suit was filed after President Trump issued an executive order that barred the use of federal funds for medical procedures or treatments for transgender inmates who are in Bureau of Prisons custody.

In response to Mr. Trump's directive, the Bureau of Prisons issued a new policy in February stating that it would not provide surgeries or hormone therapy to address gender dysphoria. Inmates who were receiving hormone treatments could be put on a tapering plan that would eventually lead to a discontinuation of the interventions.
Under the new rules, the Bureau of Prisons will also no longer provide any social accommodations, such as breast padding, binders, wigs and makeup, to inmates with gender dysphoria.

In a memo accompanying the policy, the Bureau of Prisons cited Mr. Trump's executive order and said it changed its rules to "reflect treatment for gender dysphoria that is more aligned with the latest scientific information, that is consistent with BOP's longstanding policy of providing medical care that is tailored to the unique needs of the inmate, and that accounts for the complex security and administration concerns in the correctional environment."

In June, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth issued an order preventing the Trump administration from enforcing the February policy. The judge required the Bureau of Prisons to continue providing medical interventions and social accommodations to a class of inmates with gender dysphoria.

"The court does not wade into the culture war being waged against transgender individuals," Lamberth, who was appointed by President Ronald Reagan, wrote in a 31-page decision. "The court simply concludes that the government violated [federal law] when it issued a new policy restricting the provision of gender-affirming care to inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria."
Lamberth issued an order in August that continued to block the policy.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit then declined to lift the district court's injunction. In a 2-1 decision, the appeals court said the Bureau of Prisons "did not adequately consider its own experience providing gender-affirming care under its prior policy" and failed to make a strong showing that it is likely to succeed on the merits of the case.
Appeal to Supreme Court
In its emergency appeal to the Supreme Court, Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that the district court's decision "prevents the application of the Executive's chosen policy" on a broad basis.

Sauer defended the legality of the policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates and said the Bureau of Prisons "seasonably considered its prior experience both in determining that such interventions are not medically necessary and in determining that security and prison-administration concerns independently justified a change in policy."

But the challengers of the administration's new rules argued the Trump administration failed to put forth any evidence indicating whether healthcare providers for the Bureau of Prisons found the now-restricted medical treatments to be effective, ineffective or harmful.

"BOP cut off treatment that its healthcare providers had recommended for decades and replaced it with psychotherapy — which its own expert acknowledges is backed by no evidence demonstrating its efficacy as a treatment for gender dysphoria — and psychotropic medications — which BOP's Medical Director does not even claim treat gender dysphoria, only co-existing conditions," lawyers for the transgender inmates wrote.
They also argued that the agency has not "pointed to a single security incident" relating to the provision of medical interventions to address gender dysphoria.

"Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," lawyers for the plaintiffs said. "That glaring omission, as well as the unreasonableness of its decision, make it clear that the rationales were contrived to support the demand President Trump made in the EO."

title: Ohio race takes ugly turn with Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's mom
summary: Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother calls her a liar in a new Ramaswamy campaign ad. Acton's brother says the ad marks a "despicable low" and says their stepfather sexually abused Acton when she was a child.
story: A new attack ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy features the estranged mother of his opponent in the Ohio governor's race, Amy Acton, calling her a "liar." Acton's campaign and her brother denounced the ad as a "despicable low."

Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, whose husband was accused of raping Acton when she was a child, says in the spot, "It's not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past."

Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, lashed out at Ramaswamy in response: "It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."
He said that after their stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged, he and Acton were removed from the Arthurs' custody and lived with their father.

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

The origin of the ad, which circulated on social media Monday night, was initially unclear because it lacked the mandatory disclosure of who paid for and authorized the spot. But on Tuesday, Ramaswamy told reporters it was "an ad from our campaign," according to The Columbus Dispatch. He defended the content of the ad, saying: "Every person who appears to know her the best … have told voters not to vote for her but to vote for me instead."

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, said in a statement earlier Tuesday, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."
The state Republican Party has not responded to a request for comment.

Vice President JD Vance, who represented Ohio in the Senate before becoming vice president, said Wednesday that "whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern" and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by fellow Republicans who are "whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."

"Politics is a tough business," Vance said. "And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is, if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days."

Acton, who served as the state's public health commissioner under GOP Gov. Mike DeWine during the pandemic, has previously talked about being abused by her now-deceased stepfather. According to court records provided by the campaign, in 1978, Arthur was charged with raping Acton, when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea.
Acton has also detailed struggles throughout her early childhood with poverty and homelessness, and records provided by her campaign show that the family lived in a tent for a year.
Acton told the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019 that once she and her brother were able to go live with their father, their lives became more stable.

"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away," Acton told The Vindicator seven years ago. "That was the last time I ever saw her." Her campaign says that court date remains the last time Acton saw her mother.

Her mother and her stepfather, released on bond, left Ohio without facing charges, the news site said. Warrants were issued for Cledith Arthur's arrest at least twice in the next few years, according to court records. Donna and Cledith Arthur lived in Pennsylvania until Cledith's death in 2004.
Ramaswamy's backers have launched other personal attacks against Acton, who has been leading in polls over the last month.
Other aspects of Acton's personal life have also resurfaced during the election, including an incident when police were called to her home in 2019 during what was characterized as a domestic dispute.

title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger has "a lot of merit." Here's why.
summary: Combining SpaceX and Tesla, whose stocks jumped after Musk said the companies are exploring a deal, would be the biggest corporate merger of all time.
story: Elon Musk on Tuesday said SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger — a business combination that one Wall Street analyst said could be worth nearly $5 trillion, which would make it the largest deal in corporate history.

"Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call with investors, adding that he sees "a lot of merit to combining the companies."
Tesla's stock price rose $14.01, or 3.8%, to $387.72, while SpaceX shares jumped $14.62, or 9.9%, to $162.41 in morning trading. Here's what to know about a possible merger between the companies.
How big would a SpaceX-Tesla merger be?
The merger would likely be valued at close to $5 trillion, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News.

SpaceX is currently valued at $1.98 trillion, while Tesla's market capitalization stands at about $1.5 trillion. But Tesla shareholders would likely demand a premium for their shares to agree to the merger, Ives noted.
"For the merger to get passed by shareholders, it would have to be a higher price for Tesla — likely in the $500/$550 per share range in our view," he said.

That would make the combined company one of the most valuable in the world, rivaling that of the most highly valued businesses like chipmaker Nvidia, worth $5.2 trillion, or Apple, valued at $4.95 trillion.
What is the strategic rationale for merging the companies?

The main reason for combining SpaceX, a space exploration and AI company, with an electric vehicle manufacturer is to position them for a future in which artificial intelligence, or what Musk terms "super intelligence," becomes increasingly essential to everyday life.

"There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing super intelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation," Musk said in Tuesday's earnings call.

While Tesla's primary business remains manufacturing EVs, Musk has signaled that the company is shifting away from traditional motor vehicles. In January, the Tesla CEO said the company would phase out production of its Model S and Model X vehicles.

Instead, the company is changing course to focus on developing autonomous products, such as self-driving taxis and humanoid robots. Musk said Tesla will eventually produce 1 million humanoid robots a year as the company transitions to an "autonomous future." The humanoid robot, called Optimus, could hit the market in 2027, Musk said in January.
AI is essential to Optimus, allowing it to follow orders and take on various tasks, as well as to Tesla's push into self-driving robotaxis.

Meanwhile, SpaceX owns xAI, Musk's AI unit that created Grok, the chatbot that is used in the social media app X and other Musk-owned products. Musk's planned Terafab chip factory will tie all the businesses together by manufacturing semiconductors for both SpaceX and Tesla.
Combining the businesses makes sense for a "number of strategic AI and data-driven reasons, and this is the right move for Musk," Ives said in a research note.
What are the hurdles to a merger?
On Tuesday's conference call, Musk underlined that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla is far from assured, noting that a majority of Tesla shareholders would need to vote in favor of the combination.
"I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it," he said.

Musk added, "At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."
Even so, Ives assigns an 80% to 90% chance that the merger will happen by the end of 2027.

title: Trump weighs moving White House press corps out of building
summary: Outside allies of President Trump have recently pushed the idea of moving the White House press corps to another building, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, one source said.
story: President Trump has discussed the possibility of moving the White House press corps to another building, according to two people close to the president — a move that could escalate Mr. Trump's clashes with news organizations over coverage and access.
Outside allies of the president have pushed the idea in recent weeks, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, one source told CBS News.
No final decisions have been made, according to both sources.
The discussions were first reported by The New York Times.

White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement: "America is rightly distrustful of the fake news media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information. … All options remain on the table, and we will make an announcement when appropriate."

Reporters have had dedicated workspaces in the White House building for more than a century. The current press briefing room was constructed during the Nixon administration, replacing a swimming pool that dated back to Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency.
But late last month, Mr. Trump posted a before-and-after image to Truth Social that suggested the briefing room could be turned back into a swimming pool.

Ahead of Mr. Trump's first term, administration officials floated the idea of moving the press corps out of the building, framing it as a bid to broaden access by using a roomier part of the White House complex rather than the small, cramped spaces in the West Wing. Incoming chief of staff Reince Priebus told NBC News the administration had discussed holding news conferences in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which is adjacent to the West Wing.
Mr. Trump ultimately did not follow through with the plans, telling Fox News two days before his 2017 inauguration: "The press went crazy, so I said, 'Let's not move it.'"
The idea has appeared to reemerge after more than a year of disputes between the Trump administration and journalists over access to the White House.

Last month, Mr. Trump attempted to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House complex, accusing them of unfair coverage. Journalists from all three outlets were briefly unable to access the building, but a federal judge reinstated their press credentials, finding the ban likely violated the First Amendment and the news outlets' right to due process.

The Trump administration has continued to periodically block CNN from participating in the television press pool, a group of five networks that cover the president's travel and events on a rotating basis and provide video to other news organizations.
(CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.)

More than a year ago, the White House prevented the Associated Press from accessing the Oval Office and some other spaces because the wire service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump's preferred term, the Gulf of America.

The Pentagon has also clamped down on press access. Last year, the military required reporters to sign onto a set of restrictions — including a promise not to "solicit" sensitive information — in order to maintain daily access to the Pentagon. Most news organizations declined to sign the new rules and vacated the building.
After a judge struck down the Pentagon's press restrictions earlier this year, the military announced it would stop allowing reporters to enter the building unescorted altogether.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said a "new and improved press workspace will be established in an annex facility outside the Pentagon, but still on Pentagon grounds."

title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
summary: Memphis has become a hotspot for data centers driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
story: In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city,  which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.
Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.
SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.
The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.
Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.
A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

title: Polymarket removes bets on outcome of Cornell sexual assault case
summary: The market had amassed $450,000 in wagers by the time it was pulled from the international platform.
story: The online predictions market platform Polymarket has removed a contract that allowed users to bet on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.

More than $450,000 had been wagered on this question before it was taken off Polymarket's platform.  It had been available since Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to "activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law."

"Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time," a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. "This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market."

Some of the recent outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with the platform, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several others.
A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, told the Associated Press the director had no comment.
Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour.

A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaint. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren't involved. They have not been charged with a crime.

Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.

title: We tested an experimental weight loss drug. The results were "terrifying."
summary: CBS News tested what was marketed as an experimental weight loss drug bought from several sources to find out what's actually in the vials.
story: A drug that's not FDA approved and still in clinical trials is being advertised all over the internet. Buying it turned out to be alarmingly easy.

First, CBS News national correspondent Adam Yamaguchi placed an online order through the website for Reset Wellness, a clinic started by a nurse practitioner, for 20 milligrams of retatrutide. The weight-loss medication, known as Reta, is an experimental peptide drug that Eli Lilly is studying as a next-generation obesity treatment. At checkout, he was promised a health evaluation, but the product arrived a week later without ever having to speak to a health professional.

Next, he purchased Reta from the website for Bodystreet Jupiter, a gym in Florida, after confirming he met its Body Mass Index, or BMI, requirement. The site said a doctor would review his intake form. The product arrived two days later without a consultation.
He even found a poster advertising the product for sale over the counter, at a bodega in Brooklyn.
Yamaguchi was able to buy a vial labeled "Retatrutide" at the corner store for $90. It came with a warning on the label that read "Research use only, not for human consumption."

Dr. Reshma Ramachandran, a Yale physician who has studied the growing use of peptides and weight loss medications, said it's "astounding" how easily accessible these drugs are. She said people who try products labeled as retatrutide are essentially acting as guinea pigs, because the drug is still in clinical trials and has not been certified as safe and effective.
She said prescribing a drug should involve a conversation about a patient's medical history, the risks and whether the treatment is appropriate.
What's actually in the vials?
University of Iowa research scientist Jason Galpin analyzed the samples for CBS News.
Both samples Yamaguchi bought online were consistent with a basic standard Galpin created for retatrutide, which isn't the same as the drug being studied in Eli Lilly's clinical trials.
But the bodega sample didn't appear to even contain a peptide at all.
"It does not look anything like a peptide," Galpin said of the sample Yamaguchi bought at a Brooklyn corner store, which was labeled as Reta.
Instead, Galpin found a compound called phenylacetic acid, which he described as a filler. It's commonly found in fragrances and lip balms.
Further testing by Carl Ross, director of development at the University of Iowa's Center for Biocatalysis and Bioprocessing, found 13 colonies of bacteria in the sample.
He warned that injecting material contaminated with bacteria could cause an infection.
"As kids, we're all taught to wash out cuts if we get cut, but in this case … we're injecting bacteria under the skin where it could multiply," Ross said. "It's pretty terrifying."
Ramachandran shared the concern.
"What's frightening to hear is that someone who's buying this, who's spending money on this, is going to potentially get themselves very sick," she said.
Ramachandran said she hopes regulators can find ways to oversee these platforms as access to unapproved drugs continues to grow.

"I am trying to be hopeful that there might be ways to regulate these platforms… like the horse is out of the barn and so we're going to be trying to catch up to what's our current reality of really easy access"
CBS News has reached out to INDR Labs, Reset, Bodystreet for comment. They have not yet responded.
A spokesperson for Eli Lilly sent CBS News the following statement:

"Regulated manufacturers must demonstrate quality and consistency, dose after dose. Black-market sellers do not. A single test is a snapshot, not a guarantee that the dose will be sterile or stable in two weeks, let alone that the next vial will be safe. Giving consumers false confidence in unregulated products based on limited testing risks putting more people in harm's way. Every day FDA, DOJ and other authorities fail to act against the growing black market is another day unsuspecting consumers are put at risk.

Third-party testing of a single sample with unknown ingredients and origin does not make an illegal product safe. Neither does taking a previous dose without apparent harm. Consumers are gambling with their health, with no way of knowing when a dangerous vial may arrive at their door. CBS itself recently reported on two deaths associated with black-market retatrutide, while media outlets in the UK, Ireland, an Australia have reported serious injuries and at least one death associated with similar illicit products. Just this week, Bloomberg reported that two manufacturers formerly on FDA's Green List had been laundering product from other sources, had been contaminated with black mold and bugs, and had been destroying records."

Jamie  Korenblat and 
                                                  
                                  Daniel  Gilbert
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Cornell responds to Jane Doe letter saying she felt disbelieved
summary: Cornell has denied claims made in a letter from a former student, known as Jane Doe, about a remark by the school's president.
story: The former Cornell student known as Jane Doe has sent a letter to the school saying she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by the university's president, Michael Kotlikoff, after she accused multiple men of sexually assaulting her at a fraternity house in 2024.
In a statement Tuesday, Cornell disputed her account of Kotlikoff's comments.

The letter, obtained by CBS News, was sent earlier this month to Cornell's Faculty Senate as it considers a no-confidence vote in Kotlikoff's administration. In the letter, Jane Doe describes what she calls "a second-hand account" of a conversation between Kotlikoff and the then-president of Cornell's Tri Delta sorority chapter.

"After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff's initial response was along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'" wrote Jane Doe in the letter. "She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story."
Jane Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on Nov. 8, 2024, about three weeks after she said it took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house.
The university said in its statement Tuesday that her description of Kotlikoff's comment in the letter is "incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account."

"The question 'why did it take so long for the assault to be reported' was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024," Cornell said. "He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting."

In her one-page letter, Jane Doe wrote that hearing of the comment "diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."
She added, "I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the Faculty Senate are among them."

In a statement provided to CBS News on Tuesday regarding the letter, Jane Doe's attorney said, "Jane Doe, through counsel, provided a statement to the Dean of Faculty and Speaker of the Faculty Senate regarding her understanding of comments made by President Kotlikoff in the presence of one of her sorority sisters and one or more faculty members. The letter was sent for informational purposes only. Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it.  Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate."

How Cornell and its leadership handled Jane Doe's original report of the alleged assaults is one of the issues raised in the civil lawsuit she filed last month against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its then-members, and others including her sorority at the time, Delta Delta Delta.
CBS News has reached out to the seven former fraternity members. All have denied wrongdoing. None of them has been charged with a crime.

In a court filing Tuesday, a former president of the Chi Phi fraternity was dropped from her lawsuit. His attorney, Eric Bernstein, told CBS News in a statement that his client wasn't serving as president of the fraternity at the time of the alleged assault.
"We're not validating or commenting on the charges or the allegations themselves but they had the wrong guy here. We're happy with the outcome," Bernstein said in the statement.

Jared  Ochacher
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Cornell faculty member alleges "silencing of Jane Doe's voice"
summary: Some Cornell faculty members say a letter from Jane Doe in which she said she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by university president Michael Kotlikoff was not shared with them.
story: Some Cornell faculty members say a letter from Jane Doe in which she said she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by university president Michael Kotlikoff was not shared with them.
One faculty member called that a "silencing of Jane Doe's voice."

Doe has filed a lawsuit alleging gang rape at a 2024 fraternity party. The allegations have started a firestorm of controversy and prompted a criminal investigation as well as an independent review at Cornell over how it handled her allegations.

The letter from Doe was dated Oct. 14 and sent to Cornell faculty leaders. That's the same day members of the Faculty Senate began debating a possible no-confidence vote in Kotlikoff's administration.

In the letter, Doe says she felt "disbelieved" by Kotlikoff. The letter also asks the faculty be made aware of its contents. Doe says she's not trying to tell the faculty how to vote, she just wants them to have this information before they vote.
However, three Cornell faculty sources tell CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi they never received the letter from university administration.
"I think what's the most important at this point is that the Faculty Senate did not receive that letter from Jane Doe," Cornell Faculty Senate member Risa Lieberwitz said.
Lieberwitz said because the Faculty Senate didn't receive the letter from Doe, they may have missed the opportunity to question Kotlikoff directly about it.
"What we have is the silencing of Jane Doe's voice to the Faculty Senate when we were meeting and when we had the opportunity to ask about it," Lieberwitz said.
The university says the dean of faculty sent the letter to general counsel for verification and then shared it with the independent review.

"Now we have an administrator responding through a spokesperson who is saying this is what I recorded in my notes. And I think that there's a real question, once again, of transparency," Lieberwitz said.

CBS News New York obtained a copy of the letter through another university source. It describes a conversation that Doe says was relayed to her by her former sorority president who claimed Kotlikoff questioned why Doe didn't come forward with her allegations sooner. The letter goes on to say that, as a result, Doe "felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff."
Cornell disputes the secondhand account the letter references, saying Kotlikoff was questioning why bystanders didn't report the incident sooner, not Doe.

"Jane Doe, through counsel, provided a statement to the Dean of Faculty and Speaker of the Faculty Senate regarding her understanding of comments made by President Kotlikoff in the presence of one of her sorority sisters and one or more faculty members.  The letter was sent for informational purposes only. Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it.  Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate," Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra said in a statement.

Multiple faculty members told CBS News New York the letter should have been shared with them. Lieberwitz said it was fortunate they received the letter before the second meeting to discuss a no-confidence vote on Oct. 24.
As of right now, Kotlikoff is not scheduled to be present at that meeting, members of the Faculty Senate told CBS News New York.
Associate Professor David Bateman of the American Association of University Professors supports a vote of no-confidence.

"Why I've come out in favor of a no-confidence vote, is simply that I was not persuaded after that meeting that the university administration is actually going to change its structures to listen to students and to faculty in a serious, deliberative way," Bateman said.

Tuesday, former Acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates, who has been appointed by Cornell to lead a review of the university's handling of sexual assault allegations, sent an email which CBS News New York obtained from a member of the Cornell community who received it. In the email, Yates promises to review the university's response to Doe's allegations and Cornell's sexual harassment and assault policies as well as make recommendations from its findings.
All seven men accused of wrongdoing in Doe's lawsuit deny the allegations.

title: Trump says U.S. will pay fraud whistleblowers, and he'll decide who is paid
summary: President Trump said successful whistleblowers will get 1% of any fraud they report, although there may be limits.
story: Washington — President Trump on Tuesday announced the federal government will compensate whistleblowers who report people defrauding the U.S. government and taxpayers, but said he will decide who gets paid.

"I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," the president said during his Oval Office announcement with Vice President JD Vance, who heads up the administration's fraud task force, beside him. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving and I'll determine — and I will be very generous, believe me."

Through the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, Mr. Trump said whistleblowers, who can be ordinary citizens, will be eligible to receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, even if the reported fraud is $100 billion. America.gov/fraud, however, says successful whistleblowers will be paid up to $30,000, dependent upon the report resulting in criminal charges. Asked by CBS News for clarification, Mr. Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, and criminal charges aren't necessary.
"That's the answer. I quit while I'm ahead," Vance joked.
The president promised to be "fair" in his decisions.

"You'll get your money immediately, but I'll make the determination," he continued. "So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they'll split it or maybe whatever, but I'll make that determination."

The America.gov/fraud website says reports are encrypted and will go directly to the Treasury Department. It's not immediately clear who reviews reports, although the Department of Justice will administer the program.

The first person to benefit from the program is Nick Shirley, a 20-something YouTuber who published a video alleging fraud at childcare centers in Minnesota. He stood alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday and was presented with a $10,000 check.

Some whistleblowers can already receive compensation from the False Claims Act, which allows some whistleblowers to be entitled to up to 25% to 30% of proceeds recovered. But the requirements are stringent. Vance said "99%" of the fraud they're finding isn't covered by the False Claims Act.
Naomi Seligman, president of nonprofit Whistleblower Aid, was skeptical of Mr. Trump's announcement, saying the president "is more interested in hunting down whistleblowers."

"If the president is truly interested in rooting out wrongdoing, Whistleblower Aid invites him to start by examining the violations perpetrated by his own administration, including senior officials," she said in a statement. "We would happily work with him on this vital accountability effort to help save our democracy."

Jennifer  Jacobs
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Khanna to campaign in Nebraska with Senate candidate Dan Osborn
summary: Dan Osborn, who says he won't caucus with Republicans or Democrats if he wins, is campaigning with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna Saturday.
story: Dan Osborn, an independent who has vowed not to caucus with Republicans or Democrats if elected to serve as Nebraska's next senator, will hit the campaign trail Saturday with progressive Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna.

Khanna is the first elected official to campaign with Osborn, who is trying to unseat incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor. There are no Democrats in the state's congressional delegation, making it the most heavily Republican state where the California congressman has campaigned for any 2026 candidate. Khanna has campaigned for Democrats in a growing list of battleground races, including Iowa and Michigan. He says he's happy to help in any way and indicated he is sensitive to the message his appearance might send to conservative and independent voters.

"I tell these folks, do you really want an Indian American of Hindu faith who's a proud progressive coming out?" Khanna told CBS News. "I'm happy to not come out and raise the money for you or send an email, but they said, 'No, we want you to come out.'"

Khanna will be participating in a town hall for Osborn alongside former Montana Gov. and RNC Chair Marc Racicot and former Illinois Congressman Joe Walsh. Both are critics of President Trump: Racicot was rebuked and censured by the Montana GOP after opposing Mr. Trump and other GOP candidates. Walsh, who supported Mr. Trump in 2016, briefly ran against him in 2020 and later left the Republican Party and registered as a Democrat in 2025.
Osborn said the Jeffrey Epstein case brought the panel together.

"We all have very different backgrounds, and we're not going to agree on everything—no party has a monopoly on good ideas," Osborn wrote in a statement to CBS News. "But we all share the core belief that D.C. is broken because Epstein Class billionaires like Pete Ricketts are putting profit over everyday people."

Osborn met with survivors when the Epstein Bookmobile came to Omaha in September, and his campaign frequently describes his campaign as a "vision of a Nebraska built for everyday people, not Epstein-class billionaires."

Khanna is one of the key voices on the Epstein files, advocating the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act with Republican Thomas Massie and continuing to push for a full release of the files. He says the accountability concerns are why he's heading to states where "I never would have told you that I would be invited."
Khanna suggested that the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files speaks more generally to a broader sense of betrayal for many voters.

"In terms of the swing, the slice of voters who feel betrayed by Trump and who could swing to us, the polling shows that this is its single biggest issue," Khanna said. "It gets to the sense of the rigged economy and the corruption."

On Monday, the five-term congressman was in Michigan campaigning with William Lawrence, who is attempting to unseat GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan's 7th Congressional District. He also campaigned with Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire.

Sabato's Crystal Ball rates Lawrence and Turek's races as toss-ups. With less than three weeks to go before Election Day, it shifted New Hampshire in Pappas' favor from Lean Democratic to Likely Democratic and Nebraska in Osborn's favor, from Likely Republican to Leans Republican.

title: Theranos whistleblower calls Holmes "almost unrecognizable" in film
summary: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Elizabeth Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."
story: Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and one of the whistleblowers credited with exposing Elizabeth Holmes' now-infamous biotech company as a fraud, said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."

"The Elizabeth that I knew completely commanded a room, even if that room was full of secretaries of state, secretaries of defense, generals, senators. She would own a room," Shultz said Monday on "CBS Mornings." "She had so much confidence, and the woman that I saw onscreen looked, frankly, like a, a broken woman."
"It was almost unrecognizable," he added.

Shultz also said he believes Holmes misled Nathan Fielder, who directed the documentary alongside Lance Oppenheim, when at one point in the film she pulled out what she claimed was Theranos' blood-testing device.

"She brings out the Theranos device, and she lays it across the table and all of its components, so you know you can see everything," said Shultz. "But my problem was: that was not the device that I worked with 12 hours a day. That was not the device that we hid from regulators. That was not the device that failed quality controls. That was not the device that we used to knowingly give patients incorrect medical information, and she completely misled [Fielder] down this completely different rabbit hole."

Holmes never admitted wrongdoing in the wake of the Theranos scandal, a stance on which she held firm in the documentary, which brings viewers inside Holmes' San Diego rental property in 2023 just weeks before the start of her 11-year prison sentence. At the time, she was living with her partner, Billy Evans, who is also featured prominently in the documentary, and their two children.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of multiple counts of defrauding Theranos' investors, who, like the public, were led to believe that the company could conduct thorough clinical analyses on tiny blood samples pricked from a fingertip rather than drawn the traditional way. The technology was billed as revelatory for the field of diagnostics, increasing access to and costs of crucial, even life-saving, testing.

But Theranos turned out to be a sham — the technology couldn't do what it claimed. And Holmes, who had become a symbol of Silicon Valley's visionary potential, became the subject of widespread scrutiny as people wondered how she managed to deceive so many, and why she had gone to such great lengths to try to build a business on a false promise.

"She knows that she did something wrong," Shultz said on Monday. "She knows that she was lying, because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies."

Shultz was hired in 2013 as an intern at Theranos, where his grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz, served as a board member. Tyler left the company the following year and went on to serve as an informant for investigations into its dubious practices by The Wall Street Journal and various government regulatory agencies. He later participated in the 2016 HBO documentary "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley," which covered Theranos' downfall.
"You Can See Everything" premiered on Friday and earned $15 million at the box office in its opening weekend, the second-most profitable opening weekend ever for a documentary.
