"I think having that conversation ahead of time is really important so that expectations are set – it's not uncommon to find something. Most of the time, it's not something that's going to affect how long you live."
The doctor noted that the CT scan only takes a couple of minutes to perform and does not take place in an enclosed space like an MRI.
"I would anticipate in the next year or two, we will have better guidance for people who are at risk for lung cancer, but never smoked." (iStock)
"People who get claustrophobic usually don't have a hard time with lung cancer screening," Boffa said. "And it usually takes a few days to get a report back."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who are over 50 with a history of smoking, Boffa reiterated that getting screened is "one of the most powerful things you can do to reduce your chances of having your life shortened by lung cancer."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Adult children cutting off parents as some blame therapy for family estrangements
summary: Richard Blake says therapy culture has raised the bar on parenting and may fuel parent-child estrangement through an overcorrection in cutoff culture.
story: Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, weighed in on the potential role therapists play in "cutoff culture."
Amid a reported surge in parent-child estrangements, some have questioned whether therapy could play a role in the family fracture trend.

Nearly four in 10 Americans are currently estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults, including 24% from a sibling, 16% from a parent and 10% from a child.
While therapy can be helpful in facilitating communication and mending relationships, some believe it could contribute to "cutoff culture."
5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST
In two recent large-scale surveys of over 5,200 U.S. parents who were estranged from adult children, 1,014 parents reported that their children began therapy within the year before the estrangement.
Amid a reported surge in parent-child estrangements, some have questioned whether therapy could play a role in the family fracture trend. (iStock)
Meanwhile, 515 parents reported that their adult children had indicated therapy influenced their decision about the relationship, and 1,254 said their child had received a mental health diagnosis.

(The surveys were not peer-reviewed or nationally representative and relied on parents' accounts of their adult children’s experiences, limiting what can be concluded about therapy’s role in estrangement.)
The therapy debate
Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher with a focus on anxiety and family estrangement, refers to the trend as an "overcorrection" happening in today’s society.

"There is a lot of debate online about whether it's happening or not," Blake, who was a researcher in the surveys referenced above and has written a book about how therapy could be fueling family estrangement, told Fox News Digital.

"I hear it from both sides. I hear from parents who say, ‘My child said my therapist should cut you off,’ and people who've told me, ‘My therapist told me I should cut my parents off.’ How much it's happening and when it's appropriate and inappropriate is where the nuance comes in."
Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, also weighed in on the potential role therapists play in the growing divide.
"Therapy has sort of raised the bar of what is good enough parenting."
"Do therapists, in my opinion, play a role in the estrangement epidemic? 100%," she told Fox News Digital. "But that doesn't mean there aren't some really good therapists out there."

Wellington, known on social media as "Doormat Mom," said she believes some therapists have contributed to family fractures by focusing too narrowly on one person's experience, when it’s actually a "multi-pronged situation."
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
She said some therapists have even contacted her to reconsider their approach to estrangement cases.
"I've had them come to me and ask me, ‘What did we miss?’" she said.

Wellington added that she has seen parents encouraged to apologize to their adult children — something she supports when the parent has done something wrong — but believes therapists should consider the broader circumstances surrounding the estrangement.
What's driving the divide
Differences in values can contribute to family fractures, even in the absence of severe behavior such as violence or abuse, according to Blake.
"People are cutting people off because of divergence in values," he said.
As one example, Blake pointed to a recent online comment in which someone wrote, "I cut my parents off because they didn't condemn ICE enough."

In two recent large-scale surveys of over 5,200 U.S. parents who were estranged from adult children, 1,014 parents reported that their children began therapy within the year before the estrangement. (iStock)
At the same time, he emphasized that there are legitimate circumstances in which ending contact with a parent may be warranted, including physical or sexual abuse.
"Then you get into the sort of very murky area of emotional abuse, and this is where therapy culture comes in," Blake added.
WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE
The researcher said he believes the term "emotional abuse" is sometimes applied more broadly in therapy and online spaces, particularly in conflicts over politics, religion and language.
"Emotional abuse can be [about] differing political values, a little difference in religious beliefs," he said. "It can be about the words people use."
"If you don't listen to your child, then don't be surprised if you have conflict with them."
What a parent views as legitimate criticism can sometimes be interpreted as emotional abuse by an adult child, according to Blake.
"Therapy has sort of raised the bar of what is good enough parenting," he added. "There's just a massive sort of overselling in therapy of how much your parents affected you."
Wellington added that she has seen parents encouraged to apologize to their adult children. (iStock)
In some cases, Blake said, he will hear from parents that their children never told them the issue that led to them being cut off.
"They’ll say, ‘We were best friends. And then I got a letter saying, ‘never contact me ever again.’"
Blake emphasized, however, that it’s important for parents to listen if the adult child makes an attempt to communicate.
1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC
"A frequent complaint that most adult children make is, ‘My parents just don't listen. I cannot get through to them. It's like talking to a brick wall,’" he said. "And that is a genuine frustration."
"If you don't listen to your child, then don't be surprised if you have conflict with them."

Blake recommended active listening techniques, such as allowing the other person to speak without interruption, repeating their concerns back to show understanding, and asking whether they have more to share before offering a response.
Blake emphasized that his concerns do not apply to all therapists, saying only a "small subset" may view cutting off family members as an appropriate response to conflict.
In situations involving ordinary family conflict rather than abuse, he cautioned that ending contact can have longer-term repercussions even if it initially brings relief.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
"It makes you feel good, but there are consequences afterwards — very serious consequences," Blake said.
He also challenged the idea that the sole act of cutting off a parent will necessarily resolve underlying mental health struggles.
One expert challenged the idea that the sole act of cutting off a parent will necessarily resolve underlying mental health struggles. (iStock)

"This is the sort of myth that pervades in cutoff cultures, like, ‘I needed to cut my parents off to protect my mental health,’" he said. The assumption, he added, is: "My parents were the cause of my mental health issues, therefore cutting them out resolves that issue."
Other experts have emphasized that people's experiences with therapy during family estrangement can vary.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Lucy Blake, Ph.D., a developmental psychologist in the U.K. who studies family estrangement, told the American Psychological Association that therapy can be "very helpful" in some cases.

"I think people can find therapy very helpful if their therapist has an understanding of estrangement, so some appreciation that it’s rarely one relationship that’s affected when there’s an estrangement," she said.
"This is the sort of myth that pervades in cutoff cultures."
Therapy can also be beneficial when therapists understand underlying factors that can contribute to family estrangement, such as abuse or mental health challenges, the psychologist noted.

Blake has also heard from people who found therapy "very unhelpful," particularly when they felt their therapist lacked warmth and validation or did not understand the "enormous impact" of estrangement and the grief and loss that can accompany it.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Overall, Blake said therapy can be a "really helpful avenue of support" for some, while noting that researchers are "still really learning" what is helpful or unhelpful for people experiencing estrangement.
Finding a path forward
For families experiencing conflict, bringing in a neutral third party may be a better option when both sides are willing to participate, experts agree.
"Communication with a mediator, whether it’s a therapist or a professional mediator, can be really productive," said Richard Blake.
Once a family member has already ended communication and asked not to be contacted, however, getting both sides into therapy may no longer be an option.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I certainly think it’s worth a try," he said of mediation. "I know a lot of very good mediators out there who can help people."
Wellington agreed that bringing parents and adult children into therapy together could be helpful, although both sides need to be willing to repair the relationship.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
She also added that differing beliefs do not necessarily have to end a relationship.
"You can have a different opinion," she said. "You can also have a relationship with your parent who has the other opinion, and that's OK."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Popular foods Americans eat every day linked to silent brain damage, alarming study finds
summary: MRI scans of 9,000 Canadians revealed hidden brain damage linked to ultra-processed foods like soft drinks and sugary cereals, with women at higher risk.
story: A new study reveals a concerning link between ultra-processed food consumption and brain health.
A recent study conducted by Canadian researchers found a correlation between high consumption of ultra-processed foods and an increased risk of stroke and future memory problems in healthy adults.

Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans to examine the brains of about 9,000 participants, the researchers discovered small areas of brain damage more commonly in people who ate large amounts of ultra-processed foods, such as soft drinks, packaged snacks and sugary breakfast cereals.

Those with the highest intake of ultra-processed foods were 40% more likely to show these changes in the brain, which can go undetected because they don’t produce obvious symptoms, Medical Xpress reported.
HIGH SALT INTAKE LINKED TO FASTER MEMORY DECLINE IN ONE GROUP, STUDY FINDS
These brain changes can, however, be early warning signs in the years before the onset of a stroke or memory problems.
In a study testing the link between ultra-processed foods and brain damage, Canadian researchers examined the brain scans of about 9,000 participants. (iStock)

These findings were unexpected, according to Russel J. de Souza, first author of the study and an associate scientist at the Population Health Research Institute (PHRI) of McMaster University and Hamilton Health Sciences.

"Usually, this kind of damage is associated with conditions we hear about and treat at a much older age," de Souza told Medical Xpress. He noted that the study focused on "middle-aged Canadians who had no heart problems and reported no other health concerns."
GEN Z EATS NEARLY TWICE AS MANY SNACKS AS BOOMERS, WITH EXPERTS WARNING THEY'RE REPLACING REAL MEALS
The study, which was published in JAMA Network Open, included participants between the ages of 35 and 69.
Participants who ate the most ultra-processed foods held more body fat and visceral fat, which is linked to various health concerns including heart disease.
The study found that participants who consumed more highly-processed foods had more visceral fat, which is stored deep in the abdomen and can cause health issues such as heart disease. (iStock)
The study found an overall stronger connection between the consumption of ultra-processed foods and brain damage among female participants.
Women in the highest consumption group had nearly twice the likelihood of exhibiting signs of brain damage as opposed to those in the lowest consumption group.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Our findings suggest that the link between diet and brain health may be detectable before people experience noticeable problems with memory or thinking," said Sonia Anand, senior author of the study and senior scientist at PHRI.

Ultra-processed foods are usually tasty, but they frequently lack important nutrients such as fiber, vitamins and minerals, while containing high amounts of sodium, saturated fats and added sugars, according to the CDC.
Ultra-processed foods make up about 55% of Americans’ daily calories, according to a report published by the CDC in August 2025. (iStock)

The average percentage of total daily calories consumed from ultra-processed foods was 55% among Americans ages one year and older between August 2021 and August 2023, according to data published by the CDC in August 2025.

Ultra-processed foods are convenient and widely available, which could contribute to high consumption, Anand said. However, she noted that "diets high in these foods may be linked to brain changes that may lead to memory loss and stroke" in the future.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
For participants in this study, ultra-processed foods accounted for an average of about 25% of their daily food intake.
The researchers noticed that, as consumption of ultra-processed food increased, consumption of nutrient-dense foods decreased.
Those who consumed more ultra-processed foods tended to eat less nutrient-dense whole foods, the study showed. (iStock)
Whole foods like fruits, vegetables and grains made up 41% of the daily food intake for participants who ate the most ultra-processed food and 68% for those who ate the least.
The study’s findings suggest a connection between consumption of ultra-processed foods and indicators of changes in the brain.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Despite this, because participants were only evaluated once and not followed up with in the future, the researchers could not determine that the direct cause of the changes in the brain was consumption of ultra-processed foods.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We need longer-term studies that track people over time with repeated MRI scans to find out whether reducing ultra-processed food intake can slow or prevent these brain changes," de Souza said, adding that follow-up research is in the works.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump's chief of staff almost skipped screening that detected aggressive cancer
summary: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles discusses how her doctor's insistence on an early mammogram caught her aggressive breast cancer in time.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles' cancer journey and her message of faith.
Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, recently shared that she is cancer-free after a diagnosis of an aggressive form of breast cancer.
Wiles, 69, who became the first woman to hold the chief of staff role in January 2025, was diagnosed in March 2026 and underwent six months of treatment, according to public reports.
On Sept. 16, she shared on X that her pathology results from Mayo Clinic had come back clear, stating, "I am cancer-free."
TRUMP PRAISES SUSIE WILES’ CANCER FIGHT IN SURPRISE GALA VIDEO: ‘WINNING IT DECISIVELY’
Wiles recently shared some additional details of her cancer journey with Fox News Digital.

Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff, walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2026. Wiles recently shared that she is cancer-free after a diagnosis of an aggressive form of breast cancer. (Getty Images)
No warning signs
Wiles’ diagnosis came as a complete surprise, as she had no symptoms and no indications that anything was wrong, she said.
"I felt fine. I was working every day in one of the most demanding jobs imaginable. There was nothing telling me that I had cancer," she told Fox News Digital.
"I had faith that whatever happened, God was with me."
Wiles had gone in for her annual checkup. She wasn’t due for her annual mammogram until several months later, but the machine happened to be available that day.
"My doctor asked if I wanted to get it out of the way," she said. "I told him I wasn’t due for another few months and I’d come back."
Wiles, 69, became the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff in January 2025. (White House)
Wiles’ doctor insisted that she proceed with the scan, as he knew that her job’s busy schedule would make scheduling a challenge.
"He said, essentially, ‘You’re here. The machine is available. Let’s do it now.’ Thank God he insisted."
The mammogram detected Wiles’ aggressive breast cancer at an early stage.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’
"Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July," she said.

"We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist."
Emotional toll
While the physical effects of cancer treatment are well-known, Wiles emphasized that there is also a mental and emotional toll.
"There were hard days. I don’t want to minimize that or make cancer sound anything less than it is — brutal and unrelenting," she said.
Wiles credits her "exceptional" doctors and nurses, as well as supportive family, friends and colleagues. Her faith also sustained her throughout the process. (White House)
"You wake up thinking about it. Sometimes you go to sleep thinking about it. There is always another appointment or test result somewhere on the horizon."
Wiles credits her "exceptional" doctors and nurses, as well as her family, friends and colleagues, for supporting her through the process. Her faith also sustained her, she added.
JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

"One of the things I have shared is how cancer can consume both your conscious and subconscious mind," she said. "Even when you’re doing something else, it’s there — treatment, side effects, test results."
"Having people around you who can carry some of that weight matters enormously."
Everyone finds strength in different places when going through hard times, Wiles noted.
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles listens to President Donald Trump speaking during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Oct. 10, 2026. (Getty Images)

"For me, my family, my faith, and continuing to work and serve the president and the country gave me purpose," she said. "Those were the things that reminded me there was so much in my life beyond cancer."
"I was surrounded by people who loved me, prayed for me and supported me. And I had faith that whatever happened, God was with me."
CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND
The disease can make the world seem "very small" for someone who receives a diagnosis, Wiles pointed out.
She opted to continue working during treatment, noting that she was "surprised" by how much it helped.
"Work gave me somewhere else to put my mind," she said. "It reminded me that I was still myself and that cancer was something I was going through, not the entirety of who I was."
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is seen as President Donald Trump departs from the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2026.  (Getty Images)
Now that she is cancer-free, Wiles said she places a higher priority on healthy habits.

"I am far more conscious of the need for a clean and healthy diet, how important sleep is to your body, and the importance of exercise — even something as simple as getting up, moving and walking outside," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Between reading everything I can get my hands on, hearing often from Secretary Kennedy about healthy living and following my doctors’ recommendations, I have recommitted myself to doing the things we know are good for us and that will put me in the best possible position to avoid a recurrence."
Advice to others
After her close call and "fortunate" discovery, Wiles is now encouraging others to stay on top of their routine medical appointments and screenings, urging them to "please make the appointment."

After her close call and "fortunate" discovery, Wiles is now encouraging others to stay on top of their routine medical appointments and screenings, urging them to "please make the appointment." (iStock)

"I understand how easy it is to put yourself last. We do it all the time," she said. "We take care of our families, our jobs and everyone who depends on us, and we convince ourselves that our own appointment can wait another week or another month."
"We all have reasons to put things off … but you cannot be too busy to take care of your health. I learned that in a very personal way."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
To others who are in the midst of a cancer journey, Wiles emphasized the importance of letting other people step in to help.
"My advice would be to let them. Accept the help. Lean on the people you love. Trust your doctors," she advised. "And for me, most importantly, trust God."
"There can be life, joy and purpose not only on the other side, but also in the midst of the fight."
There is no single right way to fight cancer, Wiles said.
"Some days, you will feel strong, and some days simply getting through the day is an accomplishment," she said.
"I hope people going through it know that they are not alone, and that there can be life, joy and purpose not only on the other side, but also in the midst of the fight."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Wiles says her cancer experience has given her a fresh perspective and greater appreciation for the "ordinary days" that many take for granted — but she also noted that the disease has not made her an entirely different person.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I love my work. I love my family. I am enormously grateful to be cancer-free, and I intend to live my life fully," she said.
"There isn’t a day that I don’t understand what a blessing that is."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: 5 reasons Americans are no longer inviting guests into their homes
summary: Americans hosting dinner parties has plummeted since the 1970s, and experts blame burnout, shrinking friendship networks and streaming habits.
story: An ‘Outnumbered’ panel examines a recent survey highlighted by The Atlantic showing dinner party hosting rates fell from 42% in 1975 to just 12% in 2026. The panel discusses what may be driving the decline and how Americans’ social habits have changed.
The dinner party may be dying in America.
Hosting at home is far less common than it was in past decades, a new analysis found.
Only 67% of Americans said they entertained people in their homes at least once in the past year, down from 88% in 1995, according to an analysis by Data for Progress.

The think tank compared its own 2026 survey with a similar survey from 1995, noting that the two used different methods and, therefore, offer an indication of a trend rather than a precise measure of change.
LONELINESS MAY BE SILENTLY ERODING YOUR MEMORY, NEW RESEARCH REVEALS
The share of Americans who host friends or family at home at least once a month, meanwhile, plummeted from 42% in 1975 to 12% in 2026, The Atlantic reported.
Experts point to busier schedules, parenting demands, shrinking friendship networks and the appeal of at-home entertainment as some possible reasons for the decline.
A new analysis found that Americans are less likely to entertain guests at home than they were decades ago. (Photo Media/ClassicStock/Getty Images)
1. They’re too tired to host
After a long day of work and family responsibilities, hosting can feel like yet another demand.
And with more women working, the social schedules they traditionally maintained, from parties to potlucks, have frayed, The Atlantic noted.
Work, family responsibilities and financial stress can leave people unwilling to host, experts say. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
Working multiple jobs to make ends meet leaves people feeling burned out and without the same level of "social battery," Florida-based psychotherapist John Puls told Fox News Digital.
1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC

"When you’ve spent the day working and taking care of your kids, hosting people can seem like just another task to complete, even though you’d love to see them," added Shebna N. Osanmoh I, a board-certified psychiatric nurse practitioner in California.
2. Expectations are too high
In an era when every moment might be shared on social media, many feel the need to make their gatherings picture-perfect.
Some people feel pressure to make their gatherings look perfect, experts said. (iStock)

"High expectations may clash with what people can realistically manage, making hosting feel stressful rather than enjoyable," said Wildaliz Caro, a licensed clinical psychologist in Puerto Rico. "Trying to plan the perfect gathering can fuel pressure to impress others."
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS
Accommodating preferences and dietary needs can also feed that pressure, The Atlantic noted.
3. Hosting can get expensive
Experts agree that hosting takes more than just time. It takes money. With grocery prices still climbing, feeding a crowd can make even a casual get-together feel like a luxury.
5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

"Housing costs and smaller living spaces make hosting feel financially and practically harder," Daniel Schatz, a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford and Georgetown, told Fox News Digital.
Smaller friendship networks may leave some people with fewer guests to invite. (iStock)
4. There are fewer friends to invite
The share of Americans with five or more close friends dropped from 63% in 1990 to 38% in 2021, according to Data for Progress.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Americans spend more time alone, report fewer close friendships and participate less in the kinds of local institutions that once created regular social contact," Schatz said.
He warns that younger adults, people living alone, lower-income households and those without strong social networks are most affected.
The U.S. surgeon general’s 2023 advisory described loneliness and social isolation in America as an epidemic.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Declining friendships can contribute to depression, anxiety and social isolation, Puls added, and he sees the trend most often among younger generations, while Gen Xers and baby boomers still commonly gather in person.
Streaming at home can feel easier than organizing a get-together, experts say. (iStock)
5. Screens make staying in easy
Puls said that adults are more inclined to stay home and stream movies and TV shows instead of hosting friends and family or going out.
"A dinner party requires planning, cleaning, coordination and a degree of social energy," Schatz added. "Streaming or scrolling requires none of those things."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
But experts say bringing back casual get-togethers, even in small ways, can help people stay connected.
Casual get-togethers can help people stay connected, mental health professionals say. (iStock)
"The remedy need not be elaborate," Schatz said. "The most realistic response is to lower the threshold for gathering: a simple coffee, takeaway meal, walk or recurring 'come as you are' evening.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The point is not to revive the perfect dinner party. It is to rebuild the ordinary habits of seeing one another."
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Leonardo DiCaprio's 'dad bod' puts spotlight on dangerous belly fat — and how to lose it
summary: Leonardo DiCaprio's beach photos sparked a "dad bod" debate, and a trainer warns that excess belly fat and visceral fat carry serious health risks.
story: Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.
Recent beach photos of actor Leonardo DiCaprio have reignited the "dad bod" debate and raised questions about whether carrying a little extra weight around the middle can pose hidden health risks.
The popular term generally describes a softer physique with extra weight around the midsection.

While appearance alone isn’t an indicator of health, excess abdominal fat — particularly visceral fat surrounding the organs — has been linked to an increased risk of heart disease, diabetes and other medical conditions, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.
Suazo, who has not trained DiCaprio, defines a dad bod as a "loss of structure," an increase in waist circumference and a loss of muscle mass.
Leonardo DiCaprio, 51, soaks up the Hawaiian sunshine as he enjoys a beach day at the luxurious Four Seasons Resort Lanai. The photos have reignited the "dad bod" debate. (Backgrid)
"Maybe you're losing structure in your day-to-day eating … moving a lot less, taking fewer steps per day," he said of potential causes.
"And, typically, you're eating and drinking more than you're moving. And the body just starts showcasing that stuff."
BEST FOODS FOR REDUCING DANGEROUS BELLY FAT AND PROTECTING HEART HEALTH
An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk.

According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, men with a waist circumference greater than 40 inches have a higher risk of developing health problems, including Type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it. (Fox News Digital)
Visceral fat, which lies deep within the abdomen and surrounds internal organs, has also been linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, the Cleveland Clinic states.
"We want to try to mitigate these things as best as possible before they become an issue," Suazo said.
Getting rid of a dad bod
Reversing a dad bod starts with getting nutrition in check, according to Suazo.
That includes understanding daily calorie intake and getting an appropriate balance of protein, carbohydrates and fats.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

He recommends pairing that strategy with full-body strength training two to three times per week, focusing on compound movements such as squats, stiff-leg deadlifts, back rows, push-ups and chest presses.
Also among his favorite exercises are pull-ups.
"It’s a tremendous exercise that targets the stomach, the biceps and the back," he said, noting that working larger muscle groups can help build overall strength.
An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk, experts say. (Getty Images)
Suazo also recommends incorporating cardio into a well-rounded routine that includes nutrition, strength training and cardiovascular exercise.

Federal physical activity guidelines recommend that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening exercise on at least two days.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The trainer noted, however, that exercising the abdominal muscles alone won't eliminate belly fat.
"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements, but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," he said.

"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements, but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," the trainer said. (Backgrid)

Suazo said people who improve their nutrition may begin noticing changes within several weeks, although results can vary based on factors, including diet, activity level and starting body composition.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Upon four weeks of dialing in your nutrition, you will see a tremendous change in the body," he said.
Nutritional improvements can also boost energy and confidence, the trainer noted, which may help people become more consistent in the gym.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Better nutrition can also support sleep and exercise recovery, he said.
Combining those dietary changes with a smart exercise routine and cardio can create a "recipe for success," according to Suazo.

title: Brain-infecting fungus that can kill 7 in 10 patients is on the rise across America
summary: Cladophialophora bantiana, a neurotropic black mold with a 60%-70% fatality rate, surged nearly fourfold in U.S. detections between 2023 and 2025.
story: Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UT Southwestern and Children's Health in Dallas, Texas, says Naegleria fowleri is rare, but nearly 100% fatal.
A rare fungal infection that can strike healthy people is rising across the U.S., prompting calls from public health officials for heightened awareness and national tracking.

Cladophialophora bantiana (C. bantiana) is a black yeast-like mold that can infect the brain and contains a dark pigment called melanin, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Data from a microbiology laboratory at the University of Washington shows that detection of the fungus nearly quadrupled between 2023 and 2025.
LOUISIANA GIRL, 8, DIES AFTER CONTRACTING SUSPECTED BRAIN-EATING AMOEBA LINKED TO LAKE SWIM

Between January 2009 and July 2026, researchers identified 48 confirmed cases and one probable case of C. bantiana in tissue samples from 21 states and the District of Columbia. The median patient age was 68 years old.
Unlike many fungal infections that mainly affect people with weakened immune systems, about half of C. bantiana infections occur in otherwise healthy people.
Cladophialophora bantiana (C. bantiana) is a black yeast-like mold that can infect the brain and contains a dark pigment called melanin, according to a CDC report. (iStock)
Researchers believe the mold enters the body when it is inhaled or through a skin wound, then travels through the bloodstream to the brain.

The CDC report states that 88% of cases were detected in brain tissue samples and 12% were identified in lung tissue, supporting the theory that respiratory inhalation is one of the main transmission mechanisms.
DEADLY ‘FOX TAPEWORM’ LINKED TO LETHAL DISEASE DETECTED IN WEST COAST WILDLIFE
The fungus causes a severe infection associated with a 60% to 70% fatality rate, even with aggressive medical intervention, according to a systematic review published in Medical Mycology.

The pathogen has historically been rare, with the University of Washington laboratory identifying only one to five cases per year between 2009 and 2023. However, the CDC says annual cases surged to eight in 2024 and reached 14 in 2025.
Public health officials are urging clinicians to consider fungal pathogens when evaluating brain abscesses and calling for national case reporting to better track the surge. (AP Photo/Jeff Amy, File)
To make sure the increase wasn’t simply due to more testing, researchers compared the number of infections with the total number of brain tissue samples tested for fungi.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
They found that detections rose from 8.4 cases per 1,000 specimens during 2017–2023 to 26 cases per 1,000 specimens in 2025.
"Reasons for the apparent increase are unknown," the CDC report stated, calling for systematic national reporting mechanisms to better track the pathogen.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Cases were reported across a wide geographic range, with the highest counts originating in California (six), Florida (five), Texas (five) and Pennsylvania (four).
Standard tests like spinal taps may miss the fungus, meaning doctors sometimes need to take a tissue sample through surgery to confirm the diagnosis. (iStock)
Because C. bantiana typically manifests as a brain abscess without clear external signs of infection, experts say early diagnosis is challenging.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In one documented fatal case at the University of Washington Medical Center, spinal fluid PCR tests returned negative results both one month prior to and at the time of a brain biopsy, highlighting the difficulty of detecting the mold.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Public health experts advise clinicians to consider C. bantiana when evaluating patients who have signs of a brain abscess.
Treatment typically involves surgery to remove the infected tissue, along with multiple antifungal medications.

title: Pope Leo XIV seen for first time since lung cancer surgery amid major recovery milestone
summary: The Vatican released first photos of Pope Leo XIV celebrating mass at Gemelli Hospital, days after surgeons removed a lung lobe due to adenocarcinoma.
story: Dr. Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, reacts to the pope's diagnosis and how lung cancer can occur in never-smokers.
Pope Leo XIV is up and moving after having part of his lung removed.

After undergoing thoracic surgery Tuesday, during which surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, or lung cancer, according to the Vatican.
The pope, 71, has spent four days recovering at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, Italy, after the successful procedure.
DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH
On Friday, the Vatican released the first photos of Pope Leo after the operation.
The pope is pictured standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel at the hospital where he distributed communion.
The pope celebrates Mass for several members of the medical staff on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital, Oct. 16, 2026, in Rome, Italy. (Vatican Media/Abaca/Sipa USA via AP Images)
According to a Holy See Press Office statement, several members of Gemelli’s medical and nursing staff and members of the Vatican City State Gendarmerie Corps attended the service.
POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS

"In his homily, the pope thanked all the staff — doctors, nurses and orderlies — for the work they do every day caring for patients in their frailty and especially for what they have done and continue to do for him," the statement said.
The Vatican also confirmed on Friday that the pope’s recovery continues with "steady improvement in his overall condition."

On his fourth day in the hospital, Pope Leo XIV's doctors said new blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed "the steady improvement in his overall condition." The pope, pictured, celebrates Mass for several members of the medical staff at the Gemelli Hospital Oct. 16 in Rome. (Vatican Media/Abaca/Sipa USA via AP Images)
Dr. Luigi Carbone and professor Stefano Margaritora added that the pope’s "post-operative recovery allows him to carry out normal daily activities entirely independently."
Pope Leo plans to make his first public appearance since the procedure on Sunday during the noon Angelus, which he normally leads.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel said the pope’s procedure included a small incision with VAT (video-assisted thoracoscopy), which involves less pain and has a quicker recovery.
The pope has been in good health "to begin with" and is highly active, which plays a "major role in recovery," Siegel told Fox News Digital.
Pope Leo XIV arrives to hold the weekly general audience in Saint Peter's Square at the Vatican on Feb. 18, 2026. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

"Since he wasn’t a smoker and likely had very good underlying lung function, loss of a lobe, when there are three total on the right, shouldn’t have a major impact on daily activity, especially with pain controlled," the doctor added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In a separate Fox News Digital interview, Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the pope’s health status.

About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers, including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"But [the pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a Stage 1 cancer," the doctor added.
Pope Leo XIV blesses a child at the end of his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican on March 4, 2026. (Alessandra Tarantino/AP Photo)

If the pope’s cancer is Stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90% — depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said.

The pope’s anticipated trip to South America in November is reportedly still on schedule, though his participation remains in question based on recovery.

title: Pope Leo's lung tumor raises questions about cancer risk for nonsmokers
summary: An oncologist says Pope Leo XIV has a roughly 90% chance of cure if the lung cancer is stage 1, but pathology results will determine next steps.
story: Dr. Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, reacts to the pope's diagnosis and how lung cancer can occur in never-smokers.
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after a scheduled surgery, the Vatican announced Tuesday.
After undergoing thoracic surgery, where surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.
The diagnosis had been suspected based on testing conducted before the procedure, according to the Holy See Press Office.
POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS
The pope reportedly does not smoke and does not have a known history of smoking. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicates that most lung cancer deaths (80%) are caused by smoking.

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, representing about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. It is also the most common type among non-smokers.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Lary Robinson, M.D., an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the pope’s health status, as the lung nodule was "felt to be malignant."

About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers — including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients.
Newly elected Pope Leo XIV, Cardinal Robert F. Prevost of the U.S., appears on the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica at the Vatican, on May 8, 2025. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

"But [the pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a stage 1 cancer," the doctor added.

If the pope’s cancer is stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90%, depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread.
HEALTHY DIETS SPARK LUNG CANCER RISK IN NON-SMOKERS AS PESTICIDES LOOM
"We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he had a stage 1 cancer and whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said.
"Size matters in lung nodules and lung cancer – the larger the cancer, the worse outlook it is, because it's more likely to be advanced and have spread."
Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking, according to experts. (iStock)
Risk factors for never-smokers
Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking. Other factors like family history and genetic predisposition can play a role, experts say.

Recent research discovered that a rare genetic mutation in the gene EGFR T790M increased lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to findings published in the journal Science.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who were not carriers.
Family history and environmental exposures can increase lung cancer risk. (iStock)
Robinson added that other types of smoking, like pipes and cigars, can increase the risk of lung cancer, as well as heavy use of marijuana.
Another risk factor is exposure to environmental toxins, such as diesel exhaust and radon, according to the oncologist.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Unfortunately, probably over half of the people who are never-smokers with lung cancer come into stage 4 disease," Robinson said. "And that's higher than people who are smokers or former smokers, so they start out at a worse stage in general."
Symptoms and screening

In most cases, early-stage lung cancer will not come with any symptoms, according to Robinson. In those who do have symptoms, however, the most common are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Unexplained weight loss can result from any form of cancer, the oncologist noted. Neurological symptoms, like persistent headaches, may also warrant seeing a doctor.
The most common symptoms are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood. (iStock)
Lung cancer is rare in younger adults, which is why annual CT screening is generally recommended starting at age 50 for those at high risk, the doctor said.
People considered at high risk include current smokers with at least a 20 pack-year history, as well as former smokers who quit within the past 15 years.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Only about 15% of the people who are eligible get screened, unfortunately," Robinson said.

"I'm hoping that within four or five years, a screening CT scan will only be confirmatory after they have a positive blood test done at your doctor's office." That approach could make screening easier and potentially help detect more lung cancers, according to the doctor.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Experimental skin cream linked to 2-year drop in biological age in early study
summary: Rubedo Life Sciences says its skin cream RLS-1496 cleared senescent cells, boosted collagen 10% and reduced skin age in a four-week trial study.
story: Fox News correspondent Alexandria Hoff reports on viral beauty and longevity trends gaining popularity through social media influencers on ‘Special Report.’
An experimental skin cream altered molecular markers associated with aging and inflammation in an early human trial, according to preliminary data released by its developer this week.
Rubedo Life Sciences, a biotechnology company based in Mountain View, California, tested its investigational treatment, RLS-1496, in patients with eczema and other skin conditions.

In an analysis of 11 paired skin samples from patients with atopic dermatitis, researchers reported that four weeks of treatment was associated with an average 2.1-year decrease in measured epigenetic skin age, an estimate based on age-related changes in DNA.
3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS
Rubedo CEO Dr. Frederick Beddingfield said the "significant" early findings warrant further investigation.

"This is one of the few drugs developed for aging in general and with AI to show positive data in humans in multiple indications and to show a reduction in skin age," Beddingfield told Fox News Digital.
An early human trial found that a novel topical treatment, RLS-1496, reduced measured epigenetic skin age by an average of 2.1 years after four weeks of daily use. (iStock)
He believes the early results will translate into "clinical improvements with longer-term treatment."
The latest skin-aging findings have been presented at a scientific conference but have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.
SCIENTISTS UNVEIL 'LIVING BANDAGE' THAT COULD DRAMATICALLY SPEED WOUND HEALING
RLS-1496 is designed to target senescent cells, aging or damaged cells that have stopped dividing but can release substances that promote inflammation.
The drug targets a protein called GPX4, which helps cells respond to stress. Researchers are studying whether blocking it can clear away damaged, aging cells while helping healthier cells survive.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Beddingfield described the approach as targeting cellular aging rather than simply treating its outward effects.
"It's a bit like 'what does not kill you makes you stronger' for those surviving cells," he added.
Tissue analysis from the study showed a 10% increase in structural collagen alongside decreased inflammatory markers circulating in the blood. (iStock)

Skin samples showed a 10% increase in a type of collagen that helps support the skin, according to the company. Blood tests also showed lower levels of several markers linked to inflammation, although it is not yet clear what those changes mean for patients' health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The preliminary findings come with several limitations. The skin-aging analysis included just 11 paired samples and measured biological signs of aging in the skin rather than whether the skin actually looked younger or functioned better.

Treatment lasted only four weeks, so it is not known whether the changes will persist. The studies were sponsored by Rubedo, and the latest skin-aging findings have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.
"Our next trial will treat for several months," Beddingfield said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The treatment is also being tested for other skin issues. In a separate early-stage study of 22 patients with actinic keratosis, rough, precancerous skin patches caused by sun exposure, the company reported a 49% average reduction in lesions after 28 days of treatment.
The open-label study compared treated forearms with untreated forearms rather than a placebo cream.
While FDA prescription approval is projected to take three to four years, non-prescription cosmetic formulations utilizing similar mechanisms could hit the market within a year. (iStock)
The cream caused minimal skin irritation, and the drug was detected in the blood of very few participants, according to the company.

"With topical application, we have seen very little risk," Beddingfield said. "Local irritation is rarely seen and generally mild when it occurs, and no one has discontinued treatment to date. Very few subjects show any drug in their blood after skin application."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubedo is also beginning an early-stage trial of RLS-1496 for androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss.
Beddingfield estimated that potential FDA approval remains three to four years away, pending larger clinical trials.
