title: American woman masterminds $6 million marriage fraud scheme, Department of Justice says
summary: The Department of Justice accuses Jennifer Gonzalez of earning $6 million by arranging sham marriages for green cards over a decade in Massachusetts.
story: Department of Justice prosecutors accused U.S. citizen Jennifer Gonzalez Tuesday of fraudulently arranging sham marriages in Massachusetts between American citizens and illegal aliens for over a decade.
An American woman living in Massachusetts has been accused by the Department of Justice of arranging sham marriages to help her clients seek green cards and U.S. citizenship.

Jennifer Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen, collected up to $40,000 per marriage and arranged as many as 20 per year over the last decade, according to Leah Foley, the U.S. attorney for the Massachusetts District.
Gonzalez's female employees, who were also charged, married the men looking to get legal status in the U.S., authorities said.

"This conspiracy netted her $6 million during the course of the alleged scam," Foley said during a news conference Wednesday at the Moakley Federal Courthouse in Boston. "She bragged that she invested her ill-gotten proceeds in businesses and property in the Dominican Republic, which she repeatedly referred to as 'my country.'"

U.S. Attorney Leah Foley announces the arrest of six people for allegedly arranging sham marriages over the past decade that netted them millions of dollars during a news conference Oct. 21, 2025, in Boston. (AP Photo/Michael Casey)
DOJ SUES CONNECTICUT, NEW HAVEN OVER SANCTUARY POLICIES: 'OPEN DEFIANCE'
It appears Gonzalez spilled the details of the scheme to a witness cooperating with federal law enforcement. Foley said Gonzalez believed this individual was an illegal immigrant.
Gonzalez, 43, told a witness who was recording the interaction that Massachusetts was "so special" because it is a sanctuary state where "illegal aliens get a lot of help as an immigrant."
Gonzalez also allegedly said her goal was to give all her children pieces of land in the Dominican Republic they could later own.
"Miss Gonzalez got rich off selling the American dream, all the while investing her money in another country," Foley said.

title: Grandfather gunned down in road rage attack days after burying Air Force son; convicted murderer charged
summary: Surveillance video captures the deadly road rage confrontation that left grandfather Nelson Batista dead on a Bridgeport street after a scuffle.
story: Police in Bridgeport, Connecticut, have arrested a man with a prior felony murder conviction in connection with the road rage shooting death of a local grandfather.

A Connecticut man who was sentenced to 30 years in prison for a 1992 felony murder conviction has been arrested again in connection with a road rage shooting that left a grandfather dead in Bridgeport, according to city police.

Jorge "George" Ortiz, 57, was arrested after a brief foot chase Monday to end a week-long manhunt and charged with murder, criminal possession of a pistol and carrying a pistol without a permit, Bridgeport police said in a statement.

He is accused of gunning down 48-year-old Nelson Batista, a grandfather who recently laid his 25-year-old Air Force airman son to rest, in a 9 a.m. road rage incident on Oct. 12, according to a police affidavit.
PREGNANT WOMAN DRIVING HOME FROM PRENATAL VISIT SHOT DURING ALLEGED ROAD RAGE ATTACK: POLICE
Nelson Batista pictured in a family photo. (Batista family)
Ortiz and Batista were strangers, according to Bridgeport Police Chief Roderick Porter.
"This was a random act," he told reporters at a news briefing announcing the arrest — just hours before Batista's funeral.

Surveillance video shows a man identified as Ortiz following a woman down Park Avenue as the victim turned his SUV down a side street, according to the affidavit. Ortiz allegedly slapped his hands on the side of the car, prompting the driver to stop and get out.

Ortiz allegedly punched the victim first, and they fell to the ground in a scuffle before surveillance video showed them struggling for control of a handgun, according to the affidavit. The city's ShotSpotter program captured at least two gunshots, with the medical examiner later determining one struck Batista in the chest.
APPARENT ROAD RAGE DRIVER APPEARS TO THREATEN MOM ON CAMERA AS 3-YEAR-OLD CRIES IN BACK SEAT
Air Force senior airman Pierce Batista, the victim's 25-year-old son, had been laid to rest just days before his father's murder. (Pierce Batista/Facebook)

He died at the hospital.
Police credited tips from the community for Ortiz's capture after a woman recorded some of the incident on cellphone video and other witnesses helped identify him.

Video taken from inside a vehicle captured some of the scuffle, including the attacker getting up, striking Batista in the head with the butt of a pistol and taking off as the victim lies motionless in the street.

Jorge "George" Ortiz, 57, has been charged with murder after a broad daylight shooting in Bridgeport, Connecticut. His criminal record includes a prior felony murder conviction for which he was sentenced to 30 years in 1992. (Bridgeport Police Department)

A detective recognized Ortiz from prior encounters, including one in March, according to the affidavit. He had been arrested on misdemeanor drug charges in a case that is still pending. Police also received a tip from a man who also said he could identify Ortiz as the man in the photo.

title: Max Factor heir's former lawyer details judge's error that wiped out 124-year rape sentence
summary: A sentencing error cut Andrew Luster's 124-year prison term to 50 years, and a victim's letter asking for leniency played a key role in the outcome.
story: Former Sacramento DA Anne Marie Schubert is spearheading a lawsuit challenging new California Board of Parole Hearings guidelines that she warns will open a pathway to freedom for serial killers, mass shooters and more of the state's worst violent criminals.

A legal error led to Max Factor heir Andrew Luster's 124-year prison sentence being thrown out and replaced with a 50-year term, setting the stage for the convicted serial rapist's release after roughly two decades behind bars, his former attorney told Fox News Digital.

In an interview Tuesday, J. David Nick, who represented Luster during his efforts to overturn the sentence, said the original judge improperly stacked prison terms without making the findings required under California law.
The error led to Luster's original sentence being thrown out in March 2013. He was resentenced to 50 years the following month, while his convictions remained intact.
CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE
Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show that Luster was originally sentenced on Feb. 18, 2003, by Ventura County Superior Court Judge Ken W. Riley.
Max Factor cosmetics heir Andrew Luster is led to a car by a law enforcement officer June 19, 2003, after arriving at Los Angeles International Airport. (Getty Images)
The sentence included 20 consecutive six-year prison terms for rape convictions, along with a four-year term, totaling 124 years.
Nick explained that California law allows judges to impose consecutive sentences for certain sex offenses but requires specific findings to justify those terms.

Ventura County Superior Court Judge Kathryne Ann Stoltz granted Luster a new sentencing hearing in March 2013 after finding that the original court failed to adequately explain its reasons for imposing consecutive sentences.
HARVEY WEINSTEIN SENTENCED TO 15 YEARS IN PRISON FOR 2006 SEX CRIME IN NEW YORK
Luster, the great-grandson of cosmetics mogul Max Factor, was convicted in January 2003 of 86 felony counts involving the drugging and sexual assault of three women.
At his April 16, 2013, resentencing, Stoltz imposed a combination of consecutive, concurrent and stayed sentences, reducing his prison term to 50 years.
Max Factor heir Andrew Luster stands during a break at trial in Ventura County Superior Court in Ventura, Calif., Monday, Dec. 17, 2002. (Anacleto Rapping/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Court records show several rape counts received lower three-year terms rather than the six-year terms imposed during the original sentencing.
JERRY SANDUSKY GRANTED NEW EVIDENTIARY HEARING AFTER ACCUSER RECANTS TESTIMONY
Nick said one of Luster's victims, who had previously been in a relationship with him, submitted a letter asking the judge to show leniency.
The attorney explained that the woman had maintained a long-term relationship with Luster and still believed he had redeeming qualities, despite the crimes committed against her.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
Nick paraphrased the woman's message to the judge, saying, "This is really gross what he did, but I think the guy's got some good character and you should be lenient on him."
"She did not approve of what he had done to her," Nick added.
The attorney said the request influenced the judge's decision to impose a lighter sentence on certain counts, estimating that Luster could have received 60 to 65 years in prison without it.

This handout photo showing Andrew Luster, heir to the Max Factor cosmetics fortune, was released by the Ventura County Sheriff's Department on Jan. 8, 2003 in Ventura, California. (Ventura County Sheriff's Department/Getty Images)

Court records show several defense exhibits were submitted ahead of the resentencing, including one the judge ordered redacted to protect a victim's identity. The docket does not establish whether that exhibit contains the letter Nick described.
Fox News Digital has requested the redacted exhibit and additional sentencing records from Ventura County Superior Court.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM
The Ventura County District Attorney's Office, meanwhile, said prosecutors fought to preserve Luster's original sentence and opposed the reduction.

"Our office fought at every opportunity to preserve Andrew Luster's original 124-year prison sentence," the office said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. "We believed then, as we do now, that drugging women, raping them, and gloating about the crimes on film requires the strongest of sentences."
Prosecutors said they also joined Luster's victims in successfully opposing his early parole in 2024 and 2025.

Andrew Luster, the great-grandson of cosmetics mogul Max Factor, appears in court in an archival photo. Luster was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison for drugging and raping three women before being resentenced to 50 years in 2013. (Getty Images)
"However, because of the 2013 resentencing, we knew that this day would ultimately arrive," the DA's office said. "Luster reached his maximum confinement date in October 2026."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation confirmed to Fox News Digital that Luster was released to parole supervision Oct. 11 after completing his legally calculated prison term.
"This is not an early release," CDCR public information officer Kyle Buis said in a statement.
The agency said Luster received 977 days of pre-sentence credit and was eligible to earn additional credits through good conduct, work and participation in prison programs.

CDCR explained that people serving fixed prison sentences can be denied discretionary parole but must still be released once they complete their legally calculated terms, including applicable credits.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Nick also challenged criticism of Proposition 57, a California ballot measure approved by voters in 2016 that expanded parole consideration and prison credits for certain offenders.
He argued that longstanding California sentencing-credit rules already allowed people convicted of certain offenses, including rape by intoxication, to earn credits toward their prison terms.

Andrew Luster sits in the back seat of a vehicle following his capture in Mexico in 2003. Luster fled the United States during his sexual assault trial before being captured by bounty hunter Duane "Dog" Chapman. (Getty Images)
"He got a couple years off with Prop 57," Nick said, estimating that the measure shortened Luster's time behind bars by about two years.
GOT A TIP?

The Ventura County DA's office also pointed to a 2025 change in California law that now classifies drug-facilitated sexual assaults as violent felonies, requiring offenders to serve a greater portion of their prison sentences.
Prosecutors said the change came too late to affect Luster's sentence.

Although Luster is no longer incarcerated, he must register as a sex offender for life, will remain under parole supervision for three years and is prohibited from contacting his victims, the DA's office said.

Nick also revealed that Luster called him from prison around the time of his release.
"He called me like the day he got out to tell me he was getting out," Nick said, adding that Luster wanted to tell him it would be his last call from prison.

Nick said he has not heard from Luster since.
Although Nick acknowledged the seriousness of Luster's crimes, he defended his former client's character, saying he never considered him dangerous.

"I've known this person, and I've known a lot of serious criminals in my life too. A lot of violent criminals, a lot of deranged criminals," Nick said.

"I've taken court-appointed cases in San Francisco where, you know, you get more of the street kind of element, and I can tell a dangerous criminal when I see one," he continued. "My own personal opinion is I never found him to be dangerous. I found him to have done something that was crass and that he needed to pay a price."

title: Building a Layered Homeland Defense
summary: Paid Content: Modern homeland missile defense requires the ability to detect different threats, understand them quickly and choose the right response. Lockheed Martin experts explain how satellites, radars and interceptors can work together in a layered architecture designed to help operators make faster decisions and defend against evolving threats.
story: Lockheed Martin explores how multiple layers of defense can help identify evolving threats and match them with the right response.

Defending the homeland against evolving threats requires more than a single system or solution. In this video, experts from Lockheed Martin share how the company is integrating independent capabilities into a layered defense that connects satellites, radars and interceptor systems.

From space-based sensing to proven interceptors like THAAD and PAC-3 MSE, each layer is designed to play a different role in the broader defense architecture. Together, these capabilities are intended to help operators match the right response to the right threat and strengthen the nation’s ability to respond as adversaries develop new technologies.

title: Kansas soccer field crash raises red flags for former investigator who questions key theories
summary: Jamie Copenhaver, a former detective, questions why no charges were filed after a driver killed two at Wichita's Stryker Sports Complex.
story: Former detective and private investigator Jamie Copenhaver breaks down unanswered questions in horrific Kansas soccer field incident where a child and adult were killed and the driver was released with no charges.
"Law enforcement certainly needed to do a better job as to describing why these charges haven't been filed," says Jamie Copenhaver.

Copenhaver, a former sheriff's detective in Florida who worked with an FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force, is curious as to why law enforcement has been tight-lipped about the lack of charges in the horrific Kansas soccer field crash.

A mother walked away with no charges after investigators say she drove onto the active field at Stryker Sports Complex where children and families were present — killing two and injuring several others.

Police responded to the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, after a pickup truck drove through a youth soccer game Saturday afternoon, leaving two people dead and 11 others hospitalized. (REUTERS)
CHILD AMONG 2 KILLED AFTER VEHICLE DRIVES ONTO SOCCER FIELD AT KANSAS SPORTS COMPLEX

It happened on Saturday; Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, who were both from McPherson, were killed. The woman behind the wheel was released after being interviewed by investigators that day.
Wichita Police said she was released "pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle."
Police said in a statement Tuesday that they have interviewed nearly 50 witnesses, with more interviews ongoing.

"Investigators are also inspecting the truck, analyzing available vehicle data and continuing investigative work at Stryker Sports Complex," police said. "They are working closely with the Regional Forensic Science Center and awaiting official, peer-reviewed toxicology results."
The driver remained at the scene and has been cooperative, they said.

"Based on the information available Sunday morning, and after consultation with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office, investigators did not have probable cause to arrest the driver. She was released, and the investigation remains ongoing. Her release does not represent a final determination about whether criminal charges are appropriate."
LISTEN: KANSAS SOCCER FIELD DISPATCH CALL CAPTURES MASS-CASUALTY RESPONSE AFTER DRIVER KILLS BOY, MAN

"We know that this case has captured the attention of people all over the country, and many of those people have strong opinions about the incident even though they do not have direct knowledge of what occurred," Chief Joe Sullivan said. "We recognize that the decision the law and constitution required us to make on Sunday morning may not be popular. We swear an oath to support the laws of the State of Kansas and the Constitution of the United States and no one in the Wichita Police Department takes that oath for granted."
The driver had a valid driver’s license and no outstanding arrest warrants, police said.

They dispelled rumors circulating online, noting that the driver is not in the country illegally, has no documented criminal history, and no association with the Wichita Police Department, the Sedgwick County Sheriff’s Office or any other law enforcement agency.
Two people, including a 6-year-old boy, were killed after a pickup truck drove through a youth soccer game at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (REUTERS)

Andrew Ford, a spokesperson for the Wichita Police Department, told TMZ that the driver was interviewed for several hours after the crash. He said she answered questions about what happened, according to the outlet.
Ford told TMZ that police are investigating all possibilities about why this happened, including whether speeding, mechanical failure, or drugs or alcohol played a factor.
Wichita police could not immediately be reached for comment.
Did the driver suffer a medical emergency?
No information on the driver's medical condition at the time of the crash has been released.
Copenhaver said it may be necessary for law enforcement to release information on the woman's physical health condition at the time of the incident to "prevent conspiracy theories."
"People need to know a little bit more transparency as to why this may have occurred," he said.
Did her vehicle malfunction?

Police said that the black pickup truck involved in the incident was going to undergo mechanical testing. Copenhaver said the black box will be able to give a better idea of whether something went mechanically wrong before the deadly crash.
He said the data will reveal possible "contributing factors" like speed, whether she hit the brakes, timing of the braking and how far the vehicle may have skidded.
ACCUSED TEEN KILLER'S OWN DASHCAM COULD PROVE MURDER OF TWO GIRLS MOWED DOWN, LAWYER SAYS: 'NOT AN ACCIDENT'
"It doesn't take that long, in my opinion, to download that data, have one of their experts go over it," he said.
Copenhaver went on to say, "If there's an issue with that truck, that computer is going to alert the examiner or the expert that's looking at this data."

The incident occurred at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita. (Google Maps)
Why is the toxicology taking so long?
Copenhaver said in his experience results from alcohol-related DUI testing usually comes back within a day.
FLORIDA WOMAN ACCUSED OF DUI CRASHES SUV INTO PARKED CAR, THEN MAKES BIZARRE PLEA TO POLICE CAUGHT ON CAMERA
"If it's alcohol-related, they're going to know instantaneously," he said.
He added, "Once that blood draw is taken, once it's ran through the machines [investigators] will be able to tell you if an individual is under the influence of alcohol."
He said testing for other substances like hard drugs or medications can take significantly longer. Those require "specialty testing," he said.
There is also a possibility that the woman may have been taking prescription medication, which could have impacted her driving, he said.
Testing for that is "longer than that normal blood draw," he said.

In a statement sent to Fox News Digital, the Wichita Police Department shot down questions circulating on social media about whether there was a law enforcement connection.

"The Wichita Police Department is aware of false information circulating on social media regarding this investigation, including a rumor alleging that a Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office deputy was involved," the department said in part. "The Sheriff's Office has publicly addressed that allegation and identified it as false."

The department went on to say, "We ask everyone to be responsible with what they share, consider the harm misinformation can cause and allow investigators to do their work based on facts and evidence, not speculation."

title: OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush wanted to join ‘Titanic mythology’ when Titan sub imploded, friend claims
summary: Karl Stanley claims OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush intentionally designed the Titan submersible to implode, calling it a "mousetrap for billionaires."
story: Former federal prosecutor Brandi Young says first-degree murder would have been tough to prove against OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush, after a friend claimed in a new book that Rush intended for the Titan sub to implode.

OceanGate CEO Stockton Rush built the Titan submersible to implode on its dive to the Titanic wreck so he could become part of "Titanic mythology," a longtime friend claimed, saying it was a "mousetrap for billionaires."

Karl Stanley, a commercial submersible expert and longtime friend of Rush, made the claim in author Matthew Gavin Frank’s new book, "Submersed: Wonder, Obsession and Murder in the World of Amateur Submarines."

"[Rush’s] ego was so big," Stanley told Frank, "he was willing to die and kill to be the pivotal character of this story. He wanted to go [die] at the wreck [of Titanic]. The more high-profile, the better. He didn’t just murder four wealthy people and get paid a cool mill to do it — they are all part of the Titanic mythology."
TITAN SUBMERSIBLE WIDOW SAYS REMAINS OF HUSBAND AND SON CAME BACK IN WHAT LOOKED LIKE SMALL 'SHOEBOXES'
OceanGate CEO, Stockton Rush with the Titan submersible in the Bahamas in May of 2018.  (Becky Kagan Schott)

The Titan lost contact with its support ship on June 18, 2023, while it was descending to see the Titanic wreckage in the North Atlantic, which sparked a multinational search. Debris was found four days later, and officials announced the Titan had imploded, killing all five people onboard: Rush, Paul-Henri Nargeolet, Hamish Harding, and Shahzada Dawood and his son, Suleman.
Passengers paid up to $250,000 to be onboard the Titan.
A U.S. Coast Guard investigation would later determine that the disaster was preventable.
TITANIC SURVIVOR'S LIFE JACKET SELLS FOR OVER $900K AT AUCTION, FAR EXCEEDING PRICE EXPECTATIONS

Frank wrote that Rush's ambitions went well beyond his own death, saying that the name Titan, which was borrowed from the doomed ocean liner in Morgan Robertson’s 1898 novel "Futility," was done intentionally. That novel features a fictional British ocean liner named "Titan" that strikes an iceberg, drawing a parallel to the fate of the Titanic.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
Stockton Rush, CEO of OceanGate exhibitions, poses in Times Square in New York, on April 12, 2017. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

"According to Stanley, in order to extend, and to be a part of this larger story, Rush needed to compel more than just his own death, and he needed to knowingly fabricate a 'futile' vessel, costumed in a titanic name, as his murder weapon," Frank wrote.
SEND US A TIP

"You believe that Rush knew the sub was going to implode — actually intended it to — and that he killed everyone onboard, himself included, to best become part of the ongoing Titanic mythology?" Frank asked Stanley.
"I know this is what happened," Stanley said.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Stanley also alleged that "most everyone" who worked for OceanGate knew what would happen to the Titan, and "all of them are s---ting their pants" after the implosion.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
OceanGate CEO, Stockton Rush looks through the porthole of the Titan submersible in the Bahamas in May of 2018. (Becky Kagan Schott)

Brandi Young, a former federal and state prosecutor, told Fox News Digital that a first-degree murder charge would have been difficult to prove because Rush was risking his own life on the dive, saying a manslaughter charge would have been more likely.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Composite of OceanGate’s vessel and wreckage: at left, the submersible in the water; at right, NTSB images label debris on the ocean floor, including the forward dome, aft dome and rail sections, from June 2023 recovery work. (Becky Kagan Schott; NTSB)

"There’d be an argument to be made that perhaps second-degree murder, showing just reckless, extreme disregard, something that’s heightened over manslaughter, that potentially might be an avenue," said Young. "You have a lot of direct evidence of just the pure recklessness of someone going forward with complete disregard for the other human life."

title: Alabama governor commutes death sentence as doubts emerge about evidence in murder conviction
summary: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted Toforest Johnson's death sentence, but his attorneys say the fight for a new trial and full exoneration continues.
story: Botched lethal injection attempts leave Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike in critical condition, prompting the resignation of the state's prison chief. Gov. Bill Lee postpones all executions through 2026 as an independent review begins. UC Berkeley Law professor John Yoo analyzes the legal controversy and previews key cases as the Supreme Court prepares to kick off its new term.

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey, a Republican, commuted the sentence of a death row inmate on Tuesday after the current Jefferson County district attorney and several former judges and prosecutors raised concerns about his conviction.

The governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson, who has long maintained his innocence, was convicted in the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. He remains incarcerated at the Holman Correctional Facility.

"When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death," Ivey said in a statement. "My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole."

Ivey has commuted the death sentences of three death row inmates since she became governor in 2017. She has also overseen 27 executions during her tenure, which will end in January because she is term-limited and cannot run for re-election.
GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT
Toforest Johnson, right, poses for a photo with his son, Robby Foster. (Johnson Family via AP)

The governor spared his life despite Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall urging her last week to reject the clemency request and "respect the jury's decision" and the rulings of the courts reviewing Johnson's case.
On July 19, 1995, Hardy was shot twice in the head as he was working off-duty security outside a hotel in Birmingham. Johnson said he was on the other side of the city when the shooting happened.

One of Johnson’s attorneys, Ty Alper, said he and his client are grateful to Ivey for "diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution," but added that they will continue to fight to overturn the conviction.
"Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family," Alper said in a statement.
LAWYERS, EXPERTS URGE TENNESSEE GOVERNOR TO COMMUTE CHRISTA PIKE’S SENTENCE AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION
The governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. (REUTERS/Marvin Gentry)

Johnson's attorneys have waged a yearslong legal battle to secure a new trial. His push for a new trial has received national attention and attracted widespread support, including from prominent lawyers, such as the original prosecutor in his case, as well as celebrities such as Kim Kardashian.

Several former judges and prosecutors have joined supporters seeking a new trial for Johnson over questions about his conviction. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices of the Alabama Supreme Court Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers and other former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials backing a new trial.

Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, is among those who have backed Johnson’s call for a new trial. In 2024, Carr wrote in a court filing that the "evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years."

Carr said that credible alibi witnesses placed Johnson in another area at the time of the shooting. He also said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, who "claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping."
LONGEST-SERVING US PRISONER DIES AT 101 AFTER ESCAPING DEATH PENALTY 8 TIMES
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall urged the governor last week to reject the clemency request and "respect the jury's decision" and the rulings of the courts. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The woman testified during Johnson's 1998 trial that she was eavesdropping on a phone call when she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the shooting.
She received a $5,000 reward in 2001 for her assistance in the case.
Johnson’s lawyers said that the state withheld evidence of monetary incentive for her testimony.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: DHS launches nationwide ICE operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of SNAP food stamp fraud
summary: The Department of Homeland Security launched a nationwide ICE operation arresting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining SNAP benefits.
story: In the months since the establishment of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Department of Justice has launched over 1,000 major fraud enforcement actions across the country. Coordinated efforts aim to protect taxpayer dollars from schemes targeting Medicaid, SNAP, HUD, Social Security and SBA programs. These federal programs are designed to assist vulnerable groups, including the elderly, sick, and homeless.

EXCLUSIVE: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has launched a nationwide operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), resulting in multiple arrests, Fox News has learned.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirmed the operation to Fox News, announcing several arrests of illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently receiving SNAP benefits.

"Illegal aliens who have no right to be here in the first place are the last people who should be using SNAP benefits and other forms of welfare," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.
"These programs are for Americans only," he continued. "Even non-violent illegal alien crime can still have devastating consequences when they’re defrauding the American taxpayer."
TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

The Department of Homeland Security announced a nationwide operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

Mullin said those already apprehended and deported by federal authorities represented "just a drop in the bucket," adding that the Trump administration would continue pursuing individuals accused of fraud.
DHS identified several illegal immigrants accused of SNAP fraud, including multiple Haitian nationals.

According to federal officials, Rubstony Junior Theodore, a Haitian national living illegally in the United States, was arrested by ICE as part of the operation. Theodore's criminal history includes arrests for larceny, obstruction of officers and trespassing, DHS said.
Three other Haitian nationals living illegally in the United States — Wilbert Jean Baptiste, Louis Jean and Jhensly Charles — were also arrested, according to DHS.
ICE PREPARES MAJOR OPERATION TARGETING HAITIANS LOSING TPS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

Elizabeth Povea Rodriguez, a Cuban national living illegally in the United States, was arrested during a nationwide ICE operation targeting alleged SNAP fraud, according to federal officials. (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

Elizabeth Povea Rodriguez, a Cuban national living illegally in the United States who was previously convicted of disorderly conduct and arrested on battery and domestic violence allegations, was also arrested, according to DHS.

"These arrests mark the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation specifically targeting illegal aliens who have fraudulently accessed SNAP benefits that American taxpayers fund exclusively for U.S. citizens in need," DHS said.

"Every one of these individuals entered the country unlawfully, then proceeded to draw from a program designed to feed struggling American families, in some cases while carrying criminal records," the agency continued.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents walk down a street during a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago, Ill., on Jan. 26. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Federal law generally bars immigrants living in the country illegally from receiving SNAP benefits, although certain categories of lawfully present noncitizens may qualify for the program.
DHS said the Trump administration would continue targeting alleged SNAP fraud as part of a broader crackdown on misuse of federal benefits.

title: Florida puts 77-year-old man to death for deputy's murder as state closes in on execution record
summary: A 77-year-old Florida man was put to death in the Sunshine State's 18th execution this year as Gov. Ron DeSantis continues the state's accelerated execution pace.
story: Anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike. Zivot, who advised Pike's attorneys, explains the complications surrounding the lethal injection drugs used in the state's attempt. Pike remains on death row following the failed execution attempt.

A 77-year-old Florida man was executed on Tuesday for killing a sheriff's deputy more than 40 years ago, marking the Sunshine State's 18th execution of the year as Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis continues an accelerated pace of executions.

William Reaves was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke following a three-drug injection. He was convicted of first-degree murder in connection with the September 1986 shooting death of Indian River County sheriff's deputy Richard Raczkoski.
Reaves said he did not have any last words.

About 30 seconds after the injection began, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. A few minutes later, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and shouted his name, but the man gave no response. A medic checked for a heartbeat or other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.
FLORIDA EXECUTES INMATE WHO KILLED CELLMATE BECAUSE HE WANTED DEATH PENALTY

William Reaves, 77, was convicted of first-degree murder in connection with the September 1986 shooting death of Indian River County sheriff's deputy Richard Raczkoski. (Florida Department of Corrections)

Raczkoski's brother, Marc, told reporters after witnessing the execution that his brother finally received justice, while Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said that he viewed the execution as closure rather than justice.
"Would we all be so lucky to be 77 years old and to die so peacefully," Flowers said at a press conference. "That’s not justice in any way, in my opinion."
On Sept. 23, 1986, Raczkoski responded to a 911 call that Reaves had made from a payphone at a Vero Beach convenience store, according to court records.

After the deputy arrived at the scene and the two men began talking, a gun fell out of Reaves’ pants, officials said. The two men struggled over the weapon before Reaves eventually regained control of it.
Raczkoski was attempting to run away when Reaves shot him four times, according to investigators. He died from his wounds later that day.

Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court later overturned the conviction due to a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. After the second trial, Reaves was again convicted and sentenced to death, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.
The U.S. Supreme Court denied Reaves’ request for a stay of execution and petition asking the court to review his case without comment on Tuesday.
TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS
William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. (AP Photo/Curt Anderson, file)
The state Supreme Court also rejected Reaves’ appeals last week that sought to halt the execution.

His attorneys challenged Florida’s three-drug lethal injection protocol. Executions in the state are carried out through the injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld the protocol against similar challenges.

Florida's method is different from the single-drug injection used in states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to the hospital last month. Pike has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison.

Reaves' attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never made aware that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated the Army veteran as 100% disabled because of post-traumatic stress disorder linked to his service in the Vietnam War.
More than 100 military veterans appealed to DeSantis in a letter on Monday to halt the execution, pointing to those factors.
Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year.

Florida has accelerated its pace of executions amid a flurry of death warrants signed by DeSantis since 2025. The governor oversaw a state record 19 executions last year, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, accounting for approximately 40% of the U.S. total of 47 executions for 2025.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he wants justice for victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. (Rich Pope/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Florida would tie last year's record if Jesse Guardado, 64, is put to death as scheduled on Nov. 5 for robbing and killing a woman to buy drugs in 2004.
Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the country so far this year, including Reaves.
In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first time a state has done so in nearly a decade.
DeSantis has said he wants justice for victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Honduran illegal immigrant charged with assaulting ICE officers with hammer during New Jersey traffic stop
summary: Reinieri De Jesus Licona Amador allegedly grabbed a hammer and swung it at ICE officers during a New Jersey traffic stop before being pepper sprayed.
story: Retired NYPD Sgt. Joseph Imperatrice demands justice for wounded detective Jose Mercedes as two illegal immigrants accused of his stabbing face arraignment in the Bronx. Imperatrice, founder of Blue Lives Matter-NYC, warns of rising hostility against law enforcement, urging officials to protect those who serve.

A Honduran national who federal authorities say was unlawfully present in the United States allegedly climbed onto his truck and repeatedly swung a hammer at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers during a traffic stop in New Jersey this month, federal prosecutors said.

Reinieri De Jesus Licona Amador, 27, was charged with assaulting federal officers and appeared Monday before U.S. Magistrate Judge Elizabeth A. Pascal in Camden federal court, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey.
"Federal officers put themselves in harm’s way to enforce the law and protect the public," U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer said in a statement.

"When an individual responds to a traffic stop by attacking an officer with a hammer, that conduct threatens not only the officer’s safety but the rule of law itself," he continued. "We will not allow violent attacks on federal officers to go unanswered and will hold those responsible accountable under the law."
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET

Federal prosecutors allege that a man climbed onto the passenger-side door of his truck and repeatedly swung a hammer at ICE officers during an attempted arrest in Gibbsboro, New Jersey. (U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey.)
Federal prosecutors said the incident began during a targeted ICE operation in Gibbsboro, when officers ran a license plate check on a truck traveling through the area.
According to the criminal complaint, the vehicle was registered to Licona Amador, and a search of immigration records indicated he lacked lawful status in the United States.
Officers then activated their emergency lights and pulled over Licona Amador's truck, prosecutors said.
ILLEGAL ALIEN ON THE RUN AFTER ALLEGEDLY RAMMING ICE VEHICLE IN PENNSYLVANIA, PROMPTING AGENT TO FIRE WEAPON

Federal prosecutors said Reinieri De Jesus Licona Amador allegedly climbed onto his truck's passenger-side door and repeatedly swung a hammer at ICE officers during an Oct. 4 confrontation in Gibbsboro, New Jersey. (U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey.)
According to the complaint, as officers approached the truck, they saw Licona Amador reach into a tool container in the back seat and pick up a hammer.
Prosecutors said officers ordered Licona Amador to stop moving, but he refused to comply, prompting them to open the vehicle door and attempt to remove him from the truck.
He allegedly pulled away from the officers and moved to the passenger side of the truck, where they again tried unsuccessfully to restrain him.
Licona Amador then climbed out of the passenger side of the truck while holding the hammer, ignoring officers' repeated commands, according to the complaint.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECTED OF GANG TIES ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY RAMMING ICE OFFICER

ICE officers were allegedly threatened with a hammer during a targeted immigration enforcement operation in Gibbsboro, New Jersey, on Oct. 4, 2026. (U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey)
He allegedly climbed onto the passenger-side door and repeatedly swung the hammer at officers, prosecutors said.
Officers then deployed oleoresin capsicum (OC) spray, commonly known as pepper spray, and wrestled Licona Amador to the ground, prosecutors said.

He was arrested without injury and faces up to 20 years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted of assaulting federal officers with a deadly or dangerous weapon.

title: Stranger in Biden mask pulls bizarre Texas doorstep stunt as police issue warning
summary: Doorbell camera video captures a person in a Joe Biden mask eating a banana on a Texas doorstep, prompting Watauga police to issue a warning.
story: Doorbell video shows a barefoot visitor in a Joe Biden mask and "FREEDOM" shirt eating a banana outside a Texas home (Credit: Jessica Mancia).

A visitor wearing a Joe Biden mask turned a Texas homeowner’s doorstep into the setting for a bizarre banana snack, prompting a police response and a warning that pranks can lead to dangerous confrontations.

Doorbell camera video shows the unidentified person approaching a Watauga home wearing a mask resembling the former president and what appears to be a "FREEDOM" T-shirt similar to those associated with Charlie Kirk and Turning Point USA.
The person runs their fingers over the camera twice, then eats a banana through the mask before walking away.
NAKED DOORDASH DRIVER DELIVERS FOOD TO TEXAS HOME IN SHOCKING SECURITY CAMERA VIDEO
A masked visitor leans toward a doorbell camera outside a Watauga, Texas, home. Police said officers reviewed the Oct. 18, 2026, footage and found no evidence of a crime. (Jessica Mancia)

Watauga police told Fox News Digital that officers responded to a suspicious activity report at approximately 8:05 p.m. Oct. 18. After reviewing the homeowner’s video at the scene, officers found no evidence of a crime.
A search of the surrounding neighborhood turned up no sign of the masked visitor.
MASKED HELMETED PROWLER STALKS MASSACHUSETTS MANSION BEFORE SLIPPING INTO WOODS IN WEALTHY TOWN: ‘IT’S CREEPY’
A person wearing a Joe Biden mask reaches toward a doorbell camera with one hand while holding a banana in the other. (Jessica Mancia)

The department said it is aware of social media posts describing similar sightings, but no additional reports involving the person have been made directly to police. Officers have not identified any related incidents.
While the doorstep appearance did not result in criminal charges, police cautioned that behavior intended to get a laugh could have serious consequences.
COPS FLUSH HOMECOMING PRANK PLANS AFTER SEIZING 650 TOILET PAPER ROLLS IN ‘OPERATION CLEAN SWEEP’
An unidentified visitor holds a peeled banana while wearing a Joe Biden mask and a "FREEDOM" shirt outside a Watauga, Texas, home on Oct. 18, 2026. (Jessica Mancia)
"The department also reminds the public that behavior perceived as threatening can lead to dangerous confrontations, potentially resulting in serious injury," police told Fox News Digital.
Authorities urged residents to call police about concerning behavior instead of confronting individuals themselves.
"We also encourage everyone to exercise good judgment and recognize that behavior intended as a joke or prank can sometimes cause unnecessary concern for others," the department said.
A person wearing a Joe Biden mask stands outside a Watauga, Texas, home in doorbell footage captured Oct. 18, 2026. (Jessica Mancia)
The visitor’s identity and reason for the masked appearance remain unknown. Police said their assessment has not changed.

"Based on the available information, our assessment remains unchanged: officers found no evidence that a criminal offense occurred."

title: Convicted bank robber returns to old tricks with ‘old man’ mask in Florida heists, feds say
summary: David Sartin Jr. allegedly robbed two Florida banks in a prosthetic "old man" mask weeks after starting supervised release from a 10-year bank robbery sentence.
story:
Federal authorities accused convicted bank robber David Sartin Jr., 40, of robbing two Florida banks. Investigators say he wore an "old man" mask while on supervised release for earlier crimes (This video contains AI-assisted
content).

A convicted bank robber allegedly returned to a familiar disguise while robbing two Florida banks on supervised release, donning an "old man" mask and fleeing in a getaway vehicle tied to his earlier crimes, federal authorities said.
David Sartin Jr., 40, of St. Petersburg, faces two bank robbery charges after investigators say he targeted banks weeks apart while concealing his face behind a prosthetic mask with gray facial hair.

The allegations follow a sentence of more than 10 years in federal prison in a case involving five Texas bank robberies, during which Sartin wore a similar disguise, according to a criminal complaint reviewed by Fox News Digital.
FLORIDA MEN INDICTED IN ARMED HOME INVASION WHERE SUSPECT POSED AS UTILITY WORKER, 13-YEAR-OLD ZIP-TIED: DOJ

A surveillance image shows the disguised suspect during the Sept. 15, 2026, robbery of a Truist Bank in St. Petersburg, Florida. Federal authorities allege the robber was David Sartin Jr. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)
His supervised release began in May 2025. Investigators allege he robbed the first Florida bank in August 2026.
"In all of SARTIN JR.’s bank robberies, he used a mask," an FBI special agent wrote in the affidavit.
TWO KENTUCKY BANK EMPLOYEES SHOT AND KILLED DURING ROBBERY, POLICE HUNTING SUSPECT

Surveillance images and recovered gloves appear in evidence outlined in the federal bank robbery case against David Sartin Jr. Investigators say the gloves match those worn during the Florida holdups. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)
The first holdup happened Aug. 24 at Valley Bank in Largo, where the suspect entered wearing a straw hat, sports jacket, gloves and a prosthetic face covering, according to investigators.
He approached a teller, demanded money and warned, "no dye packs," the complaint states.
TEEN SUSPECT IN MURDER OF TWO BANK EMPLOYEES IN KENTUCKY LEADS POLICE ON WILD 130 MPH CHASE
As the teller gathered cash and activated a silent alarm, the robber repeatedly urged the employee to hurry, a bank manager told investigators.
"Until we meet again," the suspect said after collecting the money, according to the manager’s account.
THIEF USES WAYMO AS A GETAWAY CAR

Surveillance video shows the suspect riding a bicycle near the scene of the Aug. 24, 2026, bank robbery in Largo, Florida. Investigators allege David Sartin Jr. used a bicycle to travel between the bank and a staged getaway vehicle. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)
Authorities say he escaped with $2,900, wedging a yellow wet-floor sign between the exit doors before fleeing toward a nearby church.
Surveillance video showed the suspect retrieving a bicycle, riding into a nature preserve and leaving the area in a Toyota FJ Cruiser, according to the affidavit.
FLOCK EXECUTIVE DEFENDS CRIME-FIGHTING CAMERAS AS ACLU ATTORNEY QUESTIONS COMPANY'S MOTIVES AMID BACKLASH

Investigators traced the vehicle’s movements through video from surrounding businesses, city trucks, a police cruiser and a school bus. The Toyota was the same vehicle used in several of Sartin’s earlier Texas robberies, authorities said.
On Sept. 15, a similarly disguised suspect entered a Truist Bank in St. Petersburg wearing a flat cap, glasses, a sports jacket and an "old man" mask with a gray mustache and whiskers.
PHILADELPHIA MAN IN 'CHUCKY' MASK ACCUSED OF TERRORIZING CITIZENS NABBED IN LAS VEGAS AFTER MANHUNT

An open backpack contains a prosthetic mask, glasses and clothing recovered from David Sartin Jr.’s storage unit, according to a federal criminal complaint. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)
He handed a teller a note demanding cash without dye and fled with approximately $2,554, according to the complaint.
The teller suspected the man was wearing a mask and told investigators he "did not move like an old man would," the FBI agent wrote.
THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

An "old man" mask recovered during the investigation into David Sartin Jr., whom federal authorities accuse of wearing an elderly disguise during two Florida bank robberies. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida)

By then, the FBI was monitoring Sartin’s home with a surveillance camera. Video captured the Toyota leaving before the second robbery and returning afterward, when a man resembling Sartin unloaded a bicycle, according to the affidavit.
The following evening, investigators watched Sartin change the vehicle’s appearance. Investigators said he spray-painted the vehicle’s white roof black.
MASKED SUSPECT CHARGED WITH USING FUEL, FIREWORKS IN WALMART KIDS SECTION AS COVER FOR MASSIVE JEWELRY HEIST

title: Pope Leo XIV needs no further cancer treatment after lung tumor removed, doctors say

story: Pope Leo XIV's brother Louis Prevost shares updates on the pope's recovery following cancer removal surgery. He discusses the pope's first public prayer and messages of support from Rome.
Pope Leo XIV will need no further treatment for lung cancer after final tests confirmed the disease was localized, his doctors said Wednesday.
Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora announced the findings just over a week after surgeons removed a tumor from the pontiff’s right lung.
"The final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery were issued today," the doctors said in a statement.
POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY
"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary."

Pope Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. The operation lasted about 90 minutes, with the pope spending approximately three hours in the operating room, according to the Holy See.
"The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the Holy See press office said after the procedure.
The pontiff awoke normally and returned to his hospital room following a brief observation period, Vatican News reported.

Pope Leo XIV addresses the crowd during the weekly general audience at St Peter's Square in Vatican City, on October 21, 2026. (Massimo Valicchia/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Malin said Hamas attackers told Oct. 7 victims that they would continue attacks into Israel "until there are no Jews left in Palestine," and during phone calls to family, an attacker celebrated specifically having killed Jews.
"They’re not talking about soldiers. They’re not talking about people who, in the course of combat or conflict, would be allowed to be targeted. They’re talking about civilians," Malin said.
Malin added that the individuals now trying to justify Hamas’ actions on Oct. 7 "are now justifying the actual crime of genocide."
Hamas terrorists emerge in a show of strength escorting Red Cross vehicles carrying 3 Israeli hostages to be released as part of the cease-fire deal.  (TPS-IL)

The case against Hamas leaders also notes their particular role in the deaths of innocent Gazans during the conflict that followed Oct. 7. "The goal there is to raise light of Hamas’ criminal conduct against Palestinians in Gaza," Malin said. He pointed out Hamas’ use of civilians as human shields and their torture of civilians, which he says "we have years of evidence for."

Malin said that the ICC has not responded to either of the cases he has filed. "If we don’t shed light on that at the ICC and the ICC refuses to do anything about it, then the only question for me… is what is the purpose that you serve?"
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER'

Malin argues that though the Iranian officials, one of whom was killed during the ongoing conflict with the U.S., were from a state that is not party to the statute, because the ICC has jurisdiction over Gaza, it is responsible for overseeing crimes committed there.

In response to questions about their response to Malin’s filings, the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICC told Fox News Digital, "On the Situation in the State of Palestine the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) is actively investigating all crimes committed within the Court’s jurisdiction since 13 June 2014. The investigation is ongoing, and the Office continues to collect evidence in that context."
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. (Fox News)

The statement added, "The OTP carries out its mandate independently and impartially, in accordance with its founding treaty, the Rome Statute," it continued. "The Office does not disclose details of the investigation to ensure the integrity of its processes and proceedings and to maintain the safety and security of all concerned, including victims, witnesses, the Office's staff and all those who cooperate with the Office and support its activities."

Malin said that Khan sought warrants against senior Israeli and Hamas leaders for the crime against humanity of extermination, which he described as "genocide without the intent [to commit genocide.]"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
That warrant was denied for Israeli leaders, but ultimately approved for Deif, though he had been previously killed in an Israeli air strike.

Earlier this month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio imposed sweeping financial sanctions against the court. In a recorded video, Rubio charged, "Our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."
Beth Bailey writes on the United Nations, worldwide antisemitism, and regions in conflict for Fox News.

title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy open to freezing front lines in ceasefire with Russia
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he's open to freezing the front lines of the Ukraine-Russia war as a real path to end the conflict.
story: Russia's release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard prompts reaction from Zelenskyy during an interview with Brian Kilmeade. The Ukrainian president details negotiations to end the war with Russia, the impact of the Starlink showdown and more during 'Fox & Friends.'

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday that he is open to freezing the front lines of the Ukraine-Russia war in an effort to bring the long-running conflict to an end.

Zelenskyy made the remark after being asked by Brian Kilmeade if he would "accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country, regardless of how it started."
"Yes, right now, we have to freeze," Zelenskyy responded. "And I think this is [a] real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire or ‘stop killing’ like President Trump called it.

"Freeze and stop. And, of course, this is the minimum of what we need from Russia today. Then, of course, we will go to [the] president and to Europeans, and we'll ask security guarantees," he continued.
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Oslo, Norway. (Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix via AP)

"This is the most important … not to be afraid," Zelenskyy also said. "We need 9.5 million people [who have] lost their houses, which are abroad, everywhere. We need them to come back to Ukraine just to live and to build their country."
Russia has often rejected ceasefire deals with Ukraine, saying they would give Kyiv time to rearm themselves.
VIDEO: TRUMP SUGGESTS ZELENSKYY DOES NOT WANT TO END WAR WITH RUSSIA
Policemen walk in front of destroyed cars in the yard of a multi-story residential building damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka/AP)
"There will be no ceasefire to bring him back to his senses and pump him full of weapons," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week, according to the Interfax news agency.
Zelenskyy said on X Wednesday that "Russia strikes our country virtually every hour."

"Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people. Because of the Russian attacks, we're losing people and time. It's such a pity, because our children don't have a real life and childhood. Not only children, but all people," he wrote in another post.

President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, left, holds a paper while speaking to Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Konstantin Palace in Strelna, outside St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)

"That's why we need to end this war as quickly as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us. God bless, our strong soldiers stay strong on the battlefield. It helps me stay strong during any kind of negotiations," Zelenskyy added.
The remarks come as President Donald Trump on Wednesday secured the release of Stephen Hubbard from Russia, a retired U.S. teacher who was locked up on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Russian President Vladimir Putin also agreed Wednesday "in principle" to resume trilateral negotiations with the U.S. and Ukraine after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said, according to The Associated Press.
Fox News Digital's Alex Nitzberg contributed to this post.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Russia releases American teacher imprisoned on Ukraine mercenary charges after Trump pressed Putin
summary: American Stephen Hubbard has been released from Russian custody after Trump urged Putin to free the retired teacher imprisoned on Ukraine mercenary charges.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Ben Hall joined 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the Russia's release of detained American Stephen Hubbard and the latest on the war in Ukraine.
President Donald Trump secured the release from Russia of a retired U.S. teacher who was locked up on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.

"Stephen Hubbard, taken four years ago by Russia during the Biden Administration, was just released from prison, at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week," according to a Wednesday morning Truth Social post issued by Trump.

"Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin. Stephen is on his way back home.
"'Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back,'" Trump said, according to the post.
RUSSIA JAILS AMERICAN STEPHEN HUBBARD OVER FIGHTING AS A MERCENARY IN UKRAINE

American Stephen Hubbard, wearing dark hoodie and holding American flag, is seen on a plane home after being released from Russia, President Donald Trump said Wednesday on social media. (President Donald Trump/Truth Social)

A screen set up in a hall of the Moscow City Court broadcasts the verdict announcement in the trial of U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 72, accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, in Moscow on Oct. 7, 2024. (NATALIA KOLESNIKOVA/AFP via Getty Images)

Another Truth Social post issued by Trump added, "Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn’t know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard, a truly big and important deal for the U.S. If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt."
The president added in another post, "Biden should have done the Hubbard release long ago! What a difference a President makes!"

Hubbard, a Michigan man, was sentenced in 2024 to almost seven years imprisonment. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022, and that he fought alongside them until being captured two months later.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff told Russian President Vladimir Putin of Hubbard during a Wednesday meeting that "because of you, he's going home to his family."
TRUMP TRIES DIFFERENT APPROACH WITH RUSSIA TO BRING AMERICANS RELIEF AMID ONGOING WAR WITH UKRAINE
Steve Witkoff, U.S. special envoy, speaks at a Board of Peace High Level Briefing on Sept. 23, 2026 in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
"He's a 75-year-old man," Witkoff said of Hubbard, describing Putin as a "humanitarian." Hubbard is actually 74-years-old.
President Trump noted on Tuesday that he had been in communication with Putin about Hubbard.
TRUMP WAIVES MANY RUSSIAN SANCTIONS, TARIFFS UNDER NEW LAW BACKED BY LINDSEY GRAHAM

Stephen Hubbard, charged with fighting as a mercenary in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, appears for a hearing at the Moscow City Court in Moscow, Russia on Oct. 8, 2024. (Moscow City Court/Anadolu via Getty Images)
