title: A ‘Glee’ reboot is actually happening
summary: Rachel Berry is ready to collect another gold star.
story: Rachel Berry is ready to collect another gold star.
“Glee,” the cult TV musical series from Ryan Murphy, is returning, Disney+ and Hulu announced in a social media post Wednesday.

The series, which aired on Fox from 2009 to 2015, followed the fictional New Directions show choir at McKinley High School as they sang their way through love, heartbreak, bullying, coming out and other high school highs and lows.

It picked up 10 Golden Globe nominations and four wins during its run. The show’s soundtrack also garnered critical acclaim, with many of the covers performed by the cast making the Billboard Hot 100.
In recent years, a new fanbase has gravitated toward the show, which streamed on Netflix after it aired on Fox. On TikTok, millions of “Gleeks” continue to share clips.
The news of its return comes just weeks after the showrunner teased the possibility of a reboot, telling “Entertainment Tonight” in September that he had “just finished” a script.

“Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan] and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something,” Murphy said. “I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Online, fans couldn’t contain their enthusiasm, cracking jokes about what storylines Murphy should tackle in 2026 and brainstorming their dream covers and guest stars, including Olivia Rodrigo, Chappell Roan, Taylor Swift and Lin-Manuel Miranda.
While the show is beloved, its legacy has also been marred with a series of tragedies and controversies, both on and off screen.

Many fans, old and new, have pointed out on social media that some storylines on the show were “problematic” or “cringe.” They cited some of the performances, including those featuring the show choir’s teacher, Mr. Schuester, singing sexually suggestive songs to his students.
Additionally, three of the original core cast members have died since the show’s debut.
Naya Rivera, who played cheerleader Santana Lopez, died in an accidental drowning while boating with her 4-year-old son on a California lake in 2020. She was 33.
Cory Monteith, who played glee club co-captain and football team quarterback Finn Hudson, died at 31 in 2013 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.
Mark Salling, who played Noah Puckerman, died at 35 in 2018 in what appeared to be a suicide after pleading guilty to possessing child pornography.

Since “Glee” came to an end, actors Samantha Ware, Jeanté Godlock, Alex Newell and Dabier Snell have accused lead Lea Michele, who played glee club co-captain Rachel Berry, of treating them poorly on the show. In 2020, she issued a lengthy statement on Instagram, where she apologized for her “behavior and any pain” she’s caused.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
It’s unclear who from the original cast will return for the reboot.
Variety reported that Michele is reprising her role as Berry. A representative for Michele did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Former cast members Chord Overstreet, who played Sam Evans, and Heather Morris, who played cheerleader/glee club member Brittany Pierce, hinted on social media that they’d likely be singing with the group once more.
“Reunited and it feels so good!” Overstreet wrote in a post on X on Wednesday.
Morris shared a photo of herself in her Cheerios cheerleader uniform from the series on Instagram.

“Yes ladies and gentle men of women, rumors are true. Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years,” she wrote in the caption. “But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well…And back for more.”
Many of the cast members have stayed friends.

Kevin McHale and Jenna Ushkowitz, whose characters Artie and Tina briefly dated on the show, hosted two “Glee” rewatch podcasts: “Showmance,” which ran from 2019 to 2020, and “That’s What You REALLY Missed,” which ran from 2022 to 2025.
McHale recently posted a reunion photo with co-star Amber Riley, who played Mercedes Jones, after she came to support him at his Broadway show.
Several cast members have also gone on to win Tonys. Darren Criss, who rose to mainstream fame playing Blaine Anderson on the show, has collected both a Tony and an Emmy in recent years.
On Sunday, Criss brought co-star Chris Colfer on stage during his concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall to perform one of their popular “Glee” duets, a cover of “Baby, It’s Cold Outside.”
And that’s what you missed ... on “Glee.”

title: Vance says Republicans should ‘stop whining’ about Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad if they want to win
summary: Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother.
story: Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother.

“Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance told reporters on Wednesday in Cincinnati.

The Ohio Republican’s ad targeting his Acton exploded across the political landscape on Tuesday, sparking criticism from both sides of the aisle in the final stretch of the battleground gubernatorial race.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is running for a full term in the Senate after he was appointed to fill Vance’s former seat, said that he “would not have run that ad.”

Ramaswamy’s ad features Acton’s estranged mother calling her daughter a “liar” and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton previously recounted being sexually abused by her mother’s husband as a child, and Acton’s brother said on Tuesday that their “birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
Acton previously said in a 2019 interview with The Youngstown Vindicator that she had not seen her mother since a hearing in the 1978 court case against Acton’s stepfather.

Conservative commentator Meghan McCain said on X that the ad was “dastardly” and “never should have been created.” An aide for Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, deleted his post that shared the video. The aide, Dan Hauser, apologized and said he deleted his post “after researching it, and the disturbing allegations.”

Vance brushed off concerns about the ad, instead criticizing Republicans who condemned it. Speaking to reporters in Ohio on Wednesday, Vance said that “whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” adding that he was focused on who would win the elections.
Vance says GOP should 'stop whining' about Ramaswamy ad

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he said.
He also urged Republicans to “remember some of the ads that have been run against me” and other Republicans.
Vance brought up the ad in an Ohio rally Wednesday afternoon, though he said he “wasn’t even supposed to talk about” the controversy, “but I cannot help myself.”

“Now the media and the Democrats of the state of Ohio are obsessed, because guess what, Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”
“My message, ladies and gentlemen, is very simple: Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts,” he said, going on to criticize Acton.
Vance’s and Ramaswamy’s political circles have notable overlaps. NBC News previously reported that several members of Ramaswamy’s campaign previously worked on Vance’s political team.
Ramaswamy’s team is planning a $4 million statewide advertising push around the ad.
Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, responded to the ad on Tuesday, slamming Ramaswamy.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said.
Stearns said that he and his sister were removed from their mother and stepfather’s custody after their stepfather was arrested.
Attempts to reach Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, by phone and email on Tuesday were unsuccessful.

title: Tennessee Titans cut DL Jordan Elliott after he allegedly brought a gun to team facility
summary: The Tennessee Titans cut defensive lineman Jordan Elliott after he brought a gun to the team’s training facility in a “terrible lapse of judgement,” officials said Wednesday.
story: The Tennessee Titans cut defensive lineman Jordan Elliott after he brought a gun to the team’s training facility in a “terrible lapse of judgement,” officials said Wednesday.
Titans coach Robert Saleh defended Elliott and called his now-former player “a good man” who deserves another chance — but just not in Tennessee.
“He’s a good man (who) had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a than a criminal act,” Saleh told reporters. “It’s unfortunate the way it went down.”
Union officials and Elliott’s agent could not be immediately reached for comment on Wednesday.
It wasn’t immediately clear what might have prompted Elliott to bring a firearm to the team’s Nashville headquarters.
Nashville police were not called and did not respond to the scene, the department said Wednesday.

“The league’s firearm policy prohibits any personnel from bringing a firearm to club facilities, stadiums, and team hotels and on team planes or buses,” the NFL said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday. “The club promptly notified the league of the matter which is under review.”
For Subscribers
Elliott had played in Tennessee’s first five games this season before being listed as inactive on Sunday for “not injury related, personal” reasons.
Then by Tuesday, he was off the team.
“On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott,” according to a Titans statement.
For Subscribers
“Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster. We will have no further comment on the matter.”
Elliott signed with Tennessee this past off season, following two years with the San Francisco 49ers and then four previous campaigns with the Cleveland Browns.
Elliott’s move to Nashville made for a reunion between he and Titans first-year coach Saleh, who was the defensive coordinator in Santa Clara last season.
The coach said he hopes Elliott can sign with another team and that he’d vouch for the player’s character.
“Unfortunately rules are rules with regards to guns on (team) property,” Saleh said.
“My message to 31 other teams would be: If you need a hell of a run-stopping D tackle that can help you on a playoff run, give me a call. I’ll tell you everything you need to know about him.”
The 28-year-old Houston native played college football for the Texas Longhorns and Missouri Tigers before he was taken by Cleveland in the third round of the 2020 NFL Draft.
“At the end of the day, we’re all humans,” QB Cam Ward said. “We’re all with him.  I mean he’s a great person.”

title: DOJ IG refuses to investigate Reflecting Pool case after Trump’s false claims
summary: The Justice Department’s inspector general is refusing to investigate what went wrong with the botched criminal case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn over damage at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, including whether there was any criminality on prosecutors’ parts, Hearn’s legal team said.
story: The Justice Department’s inspector general is refusing to investigate what went wrong with the botched criminal case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn over damage at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, including whether there was any criminality on prosecutors’ parts, Hearn’s legal team said.

In a letter Wednesday to Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume, Hearn’s attorneys asked his office to reconsider its decision because of evidence of “numerous potential criminal violations — possible crimes committed solely by DOJ personnel, as well as crimes committed jointly by DOJ” employees and personnel from the Department of Interior.
The inspector general’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hearn’s attorneys had previously asked the watchdog to investigate “the incompetence and wrongdoing” of Justice Department employees, writing that the “sprint to charge Mr. Hearn mirrored the rushed renovation” of the Reflecting Pool itself.
Hearn was charged in July with causing felony damage to President Donald Trump’s renovations of the Reflecting Pool.

Trump had blamed the damage at the pool on Hearn and other “vandals.” U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro’s office moved to dismiss the case at the end of July, saying it had found the damage was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings.”
A judge later tossed the case and barred the government from trying to charge Hearn again.

Hearn’s attorneys contend he never should have been charged in the first place. They allege that the evidence shows prosecutors rushed to bring the case, despite already having evidence in their possession showing that Hearn’s putting his hands in the pool did not cause “any harm or monetary loss” — necessary elements of the felony he was charged with.

They also cited an incident in the grand jury proceeding where a witness for the government “testified — truthfully — that the repairs were needed regardless of any actions by Mr. Hearn, that the witness did not know whether Mr. Hearn damaged the Reflecting Pool lining in any way, and that the witness could not quantify any incremental cost of repair caused by Mr. Hearn’s actions.”

“Evidently disappointed with the testimony and realizing that it was fatal to its case, the government appears to have caused the witness to change that testimony,” the letter said. “After a 21-minute off-the record break, the witness returned to the stand and — after previously being unable to testify that Mr. Hearn caused any monetary damage whatsoever — the witness now testified that the damage was ‘definitely’ $1,000 or more,” the threshold needed to bring a felony charge.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The letter also said the inspector general needs to investigate “whether prosecutors knowingly caused the witness to change his testimony on the magnitude-of-loss issue and to provide the false testimony the government needed to be able to charge a felony.”
It also asked the inspector general to look into Pirro’s public comments about the case, which it said were prejudicial.

“It is now undisputed — by everyone except President Trump —that Mr. Hearn should never have been arrested and certainly should not have been indicted. The OIG must now investigate whether the DOJ personnel responsible for this travesty engaged in misconduct that violated Mr. Hearn’s civil rights,” the letter says.

Hearn’s attorneys first asked the inspector general to investigate the case earlier this month. The new letter said the IG responded that it would not open an investigation and the matter was one for the department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, which has authority to investigate “certain categories of misconduct committed by DOJ lawyers.”
Hearn’s lawyers noted that office does not have criminal jurisdiction and has been gutted by the Trump administration, with the number of personnel cut in half.

The “plain fact is that OPR is no longer a fully functioning entity capable of conducting rigorous oversight. Recent reporting has documented that the number of new OPR investigations is at a 20-year low at the same time as the number of complaints is spiraling to unprecedented levels,” the letter says, adding that if the inspector general doesn’t step in, “the investigation will simply not take place.”
The letter said the Interior Department inspector general’s office is investigating Hearn’s allegations about their personnel.
Trump fired 18 inspectors general upon his return to office last year, including that of the Interior Department.

Inspectors general are typically considered to be independent figures within government agencies, and are expected to investigate allegations of waste, fraud and abuse of power within their departments.
The president said at the time of the firings that “I did it because it’s a very common thing to do,” despite the abrupt terminations being highly unusual.
“Some people thought that some were unfair or were not doing the job. It’s a very standard thing to do,” Trump said.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump policy restricting treatment for transgender inmates
summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said the Trump administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison.
story: WASHINGTON — In a blow to President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court on Wednesday said his administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison.

The justices in a brief order rejected an emergency application filed by the administration that sought to block a lower court injunction against the proposal. The court order included no explanation, saying only that two conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, would have granted it.
There are about 1,000 transgender inmates in federal custody.

“This is a critical ruling for our clients and all transgender people in Bureau of Prisons custody,” Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement.
“The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights,” she added.

The policy, which will continue to be litigated over in lower courts, is part of President Donald Trump’s broader effort to roll back moves to expand transgender rights. It was announced in line with his January 2025 executive order telling federal agencies not to acknowledge the concept of gender identity outside of the “immutable biological classification” of male or female.

“This order is a loss for common sense,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said in a statement. The administration will continue its efforts to “protect countless Americans from these dangerous, life-altering medical practices,” she added.

In several different announcements, the Bureau of Prisons over the last 18 months has said it will not provide gender transition surgery, hormone treatments or “social accommodations” such as wigs, padding or makeup.

That rolled back previous policies that allowed for gender-affirming care, with the government saying that such treatments have recently been called into question by medical professionals. That claim is heavily contested by transgender rights advocates.
If the policy had gone into effect, the only treatment transgender inmates would have been able to receive would be mental health services and potentially medications like antidepressants.

A group of transgender inmates sued, arguing the government had failed to adequately explain the change. They also alleged a violation of the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment, which bars cruel and unusual punishment.
The lead plaintiffs in the case, Alishea Kingdom, Jas Kapule and Solo Nichols, have all been receiving hormone treatment for several years.
For Subscribers

Washington-based U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the current policy in a ruling earlier this year, concluding that the Bureau of Prisons had failed to consider the merits of its past treatment of transgender inmates in formulating the plan.
For Subscribers

“Despite providing gender-affirming care to inmates in its custody for years, the government cites in the Program Statement zero evidence from its own medical or mental health professionals to support its conclusions,” he wrote. The government provided no evidence that the previous plan was “ineffective or harmful,” he added.
Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, also found that the proposal appeared to be engineered precisely to comply with the president’s executive order, concluding that the reasons given were pretextual.
In September, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected a Trump administration request seeking to block the judge’s final decision, with the panel split 2-1.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the lower court was guilty of “substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency” and was essentially faulting the Bureau of Prisons for following the president’s executive order.
ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Bureau of Prisons has provided hormone therapy to inmates since 1992 while also gradually expanding access to other treatments and social accommodations.

The abrupt change without necessary explanation “gives rise to the inference that the agency’s purported reasons were not its actual reasons,” the lawyers wrote. “That glaring omission, as well as the unreasonableness of its decision, make it clear that the rationales were contrived to support the demand President Trump made” in the executive order.
The case marks a rare recent win for transgender advocates at the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority.

In June, the court upheld state bans on transgender athletes seeking to participate in women’s and girls’ sports. A year earlier, the court backed state laws banning gender transition treatments for transgender youths.
The court has also allowed Trump to implement a ban on transgender people in the military.

title: How to prevent a dry, irritated nose this cold season
summary: Ear, nose and throat doctors explain why your nose gets raw and irritated during a cold, how to prevent it and the products that can soothe your nostrils and septum.
story: Fewer things make cold season more miserable than a nose that’s red, raw and sore. Between dry indoor heat, chilly outdoor air and constant nose blowing, the delicate skin around your nostrils and the inside of your nose, including the septum, can quickly become dry, cracked and irritated. For some people that means flaking and tenderness. For others it means painful sores or even nosebleeds.

To find out why this happens and what you can do about it, I spoke with two ear, nose and throat doctors (ENTs). Below, they explain what causes nasal irritation during colder months, the simple habits that can help prevent it and the products for soothing and healing your nose if irritation has already set in, especially when you’re sick.
The best products to soothe irritation inside your nose

I rounded up products that can help soothe existing irritation or prevent it from starting, both inside and around the nose. All of them fall into product categories the ENT doctors I spoke with recommended, so you can feel confident adding them to your cold-season routine.

The former can moisturize the nose and thin excess mucus. The latter can cause decongestion, but tends to have mild irritation.” This one falls into the former category and shoppers say they love how easy it is to use the point-and-pump bottle.

“Gentle nose-blowing with soft and fragrance-free tissues can also help clear excess mucus,” says Salvador. “This helps to reduce nasal drainage, which can irritate the skin outside the nose.” These tissues are thick, three-ply and fragrance-free, so they’re gentle enough for a nose that’s already raw from constant blowing. They’re also sturdy enough to hold up to a big sneeze without tearing.

This cool mist humidifier can help keep your nose hydrated as you sleep. It is designed to automatically shut off when the device detects it has run out of water and the essential oil tray also lets the machine double as a diffuser to add a pleasant scent throughout your home. Also nice: It is slim and tall, which means it doesn’t take up too much surface area on a counter or side table.
Why does the inside of your nose get irritated when you have a cold?

Catching a cold doesn’t just leave you congested. It can set off a chain reaction inside your nose that can leave the tissue there swollen, tender and raw. Much of that discomfort comes from your body’s own defenses working overtime.

“During a cold, any of the 200 viruses that can cause such an infection enter the nose. This results in the white blood cells in the area causing swelling and inflammation to the nasal tissues,” says Salvador. “These then release specific cell messengers that dilate blood vessels (so more immune cells can reach the infected site) and increase mucus production (to trap virus particles). However, the swelling and mucus production can cause the nasal tissues to feel irritated.”

All that extra mucus creates a second problem: constant wiping and blowing. “When you create more snot or mucus, it causes you to blow, wipe, rub the nose more, which can irritate the delicate skin and lining of the nose, including the septum,” says Herman. “Then, dry indoor air can make the problem even worse.”
How can you stop the inside of your nose from getting irritated when you have a cold?

The good news is that a few small habits can go a long way toward keeping your nose comfortable while you recover. “The best way to avoid an irritated nose is moisture and treating your delicate nasal tissue with care,” says Herman. “Try gently blowing your nose, rather than repeatedly wiping or aggressively blowing. Saline nasal spray can help keep the nasal lining moist and loosen mucus so you don’t have to work as hard to clear your nose.”

Adding moisture to your environment, and to your body, helps too. “A humidifier, especially while you sleep, and keeping yourself hydrated can also help,” says Herman. Running one overnight can counteract the dry indoor heat that tends to make irritation worse during colder months.

title: Mom whose son was found alive in morgue speaks out: ‘It’s an unexplainable feeling’
summary: Alexus Fiordilino said she thought her 18-month-old son, Vincent, was still breathing when she gave him a final hug, but the emergency room doctor insisted he was gone.
story: The mother of a toddler found alive in an Arizona hospital morgue in February more than five hours after he was pronounced dead said Wednesday she thought she heard him breathing when she hugged him goodbye.

But instead of listening to her gut, Alexus Fiordilino said, she believed the doctor who told her those were 18-month-old Vincent’s last gasps and that any further attempts to save him would just prolong his agony.
“As a mom you don’t want to hear that,” Fiordilino, 30, said in an interview. “I didn’t want him to suffer. It seemed to be they’d done everything they could. And then he called it.”
Fiordilino was referring to Dr. Aryan Toosi, who pronounced Vincent dead at 6:20 p.m. on Super Bowl Sunday at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Arizona.

A little over five hours later, Fiordilino said, police were questioning her and her husband, Angelo, when a detective burst into the room and told them that a medical examiner’s employee who had come to collect Vincent’s body had discovered he was still alive.
“My husband and I just screamed in relief,” she said. “We were praising the Lord. We were crying. To go from hearing he was gone and then finding out he isn’t gone, it’s an unexplainable feeling.”

Fiordilino spoke out more than eight months after her son’s remarkable story of survival after he nearly drowned in the family swimming pool made national headlines and sparked multiple investigations into what happened on Feb. 8.
The Gilbert Police Department had recommended filing child abuse charges against both parents for losing track of Vincent while a Super Bowl party was going on at their residence.
“Both admitted to smoking marijuana the morning of the drowning,” the police report said.
But Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell announced in July that the Fiordilinos would not be charged.

Fiordilino’s lawyer, John Brewer, said he plans to file a formal complaint this week against Toosi and the hospital. He said a review of Vincent’s medical records shows that critical test results that Toosi cited to justify ending efforts to save the child were not completed until after the toddler was declared dead.

“The parents were faced with having to decide whether to keep trying to revive their son, and the doctor provided them with false information,” Brewer said. “That’s beyond a conscious disregard for human life.”

Brewer’s office turned its records over to the Gilbert Police Department, which said it forwarded everything to the state attorney general’s office for review. The AG’s office said Wednesday that it has not made a decision to review this case.
Toosi’s lawyer, Scott Holden, released a statement in response.

“Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” it said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.”
Meanwhile, the hospital called the situation “heartbreaking” in a statement.

“Out of respect for the patient’s privacy, we cannot share any information and we are unable to comment on those involved in patient care,” it said. “Patient safety and exceptional care are our highest priorities.”
Asked how Vincent is doing now, Fiordilino said, “He’s getting better.”
Brewer said that while the boy is home with his family, he has many health challenges.
“Vincent is severely brain-injured,” he said. “He can’t swallow. He seizes up. He can’t sit up on his own or crawl.”

The tragic turn of events began around 5:38 p.m. Feb. 8 with a 911 call for help after Vincent was found floating face down in the family pool and a relative tried to revive him by performing CPR, according to a police report obtained by NBC affiliate KPNX of Phoenix.
Vincent was rushed to the emergency room at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where an ER team that included Toosi took over the effort to save him.
At 6:13 p.m., according to the report, Toosi went out to deliver bad news to the boy’s parents.
“As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call time of death,” Toosi said, according to the report.
Then, “at approximately 18:20 hours, Dr. Toosi called the time of death and requested a moment of silence.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Just as Fiordilino told NBC News, police officers who had been in the ER said in the report that the child still appeared to be gasping for breath after he was declared dead.

A detective reported then hearing “another audible gasp” at around 7:18 p.m. as the ER workers were preparing to move Vincent from the trauma room to the “cold room” that serves as the hospital’s morgue and where the temperature is set at 36 to 39 degrees.
The same detective said that when he returned to photograph the body an hour later, he “again observed what appeared to be a gasp or air release.”
“The nurse again stated it was agonal breathing and explained it was due to compressions, oxygen, and possible pressure applied by family members while saying goodbye,” the report says.
And at 7:23 p.m., “the cold room door was closed,” the report says.
More than four hours later, when the medical examiner’s team arrived at 11:52 p.m. to retrieve the boy, “he was found breathing,” the report says.
“The family was notified immediately,” and the boy was airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.
Fiordilino said that when she saw her son again in the pediatric intensive care unit, “he was hooked up to all kinds of monitors and things.”
“He looked like a different baby,” she said. “It’s something I hope no other parent has to live through.”

title: Officer who found man dead in Florida home allegedly moved in, renovated and assumed his identity for years
summary: Dennis West was found dead in his Florida home during a welfare check in July 2022.
story: Dennis West was found dead in his Florida home during a welfare check in July 2022. Weeks later, one of the responding officers who discovered his body moved into the home and spent years impersonating him, according to investigators.

Brian Louis Sguros, 35, an officer with the Lauderhill Police Department, was arrested Tuesday and faces several felony charges: official misconduct, criminal use of deceased person’s identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.
It’s not clear whether Sguros has obtained an attorney.
For Subscribers

The Broward County Sheriff’s Office said in a news release that Sguros responded to the welfare check at West’s home on July 11, 2022. West, 71, was found dead inside, and his death was determined to be from natural causes, the news release stated.
In paperwork Sguros allegedly filed, he admitted he took possession of the home in August 2022, weeks after West died, the release states.
For Subscribers

Sguros presented himself to the county medical examiner’s office as West’s friend, though there is no indication that Sguros knew West, according to the sheriff’s office. He also told the office that West had no living family, which is untrue, authorities said.

Authorities said Sguros paid taxes and utilities on the home in West’s name. He is also accused of using West’s identification to “get the city of Lauderhill to issue a permit to facilitate repairs,” the release states. He allegedly used law enforcement databases to obtain information about West and forged West’s signature on a permit.

Sguros appeared in court on Wednesday and was ordered held on a $25,000 bond, NBC South Florida reported. After his arrest, he was placed on administrative leave without pay from the Lauderhill Police Department.

title: Secret Service study explores how to prevent workplace violence
summary: The law enforcement agency best known for protecting the president is using its knowledge to prevent attacks.
story: WASHINGTON — The Secret Service, best known for protecting presidents and dignitaries, is leveraging its vast intelligence gathering, research capabilities and other tools to help prevent workplace violence.

A new report seen by NBC News from the Secret Service’s National Threat Assessment Center analyzed 50 cases of workplace violence over the past decade to seek common motivations, tactics and warning signs, including the shooting at the Capital Gazette in 2018 in Annapolis, Maryland, in which a gunman killed five employees. In the incidents under review, 119 were killed and 128 were injured. The report was born of the center’s examination of mass attacks, which found most of the targeted locations were businesses.

“Which is why we launched this initiative,” said Lina Alathari, who leads the threat assessment center. “To look at how can we prevent targeted workplace violence. What is the thinking, behavior and circumstances of workplace attackers?”

The threat assessment center was developed to study how other kinds of attacks could be prevented. Officials use that knowledge and apply it in other situations, such as school shootings, mass attacks and now workplace violence.

The report, expected to be released Wednesday, is intended to provide guidance to businesses, human resources officials, local law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals who mitigate workplace risks.

Alathari said there are almost always warning signs before someone attacks. While the reviewed cases do not suggest that attackers belong to any specific demographic group, they do share similar patterns.
“Grievances are always the No. 1 motive that might sort of trigger someone to carry out an attack,” Alathari said.
Retail and service businesses are the most frequently attacked, because the public often has easy access, followed by manufacturing and healthcare facilities.

The connection between a targeted business and a perpetrator is typically direct and personal; 16 of the attackers were actively employed at the sites they targeted. Others are tied through current or estranged romantic partners, she said.

According to the Secret Service’s research, more than 40% of the suspects in cases of such violence had histories of domestic violence, but they were not always charged with crimes related to that violence, the report found.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Given the prevalence of violence against intimate partners, the study urges workplaces to recognize signs and support employees.

“That includes empowering those who may be experiencing stalking, harassing, threats from romantic partners or other relatives to feel connected enough to come forward and ask for help,” Alathari said.

Most of the attackers used firearms, but others used knives, explosives or vehicles. Nearly 25% of the attacks involved more than one weapon. The resolutions of the incidents varied; in more than 75% of them, attackers stopped causing harm on their own and were arrested at the scene. Nearly half died by suicide. In 14% of the studied cases, law enforcement ended the violence by killing the suspect.

The National Threat Assessment Center Team described one case in which the suspect had been fired but the employee’s badge access remained active and allowed the attacker to return and gain access. It advised people to look for common warning signs: changes in behavior, depression, increased absenteeism, discussion of weapons, expression of violent thoughts or any kind of threats against co-workers.
Last year, the Secret Service led 400 training sessions on preventing mass violence for roughly 50,000 participants nationwide.
“There are always opportunities for intervention, and what I can tell you is that the cost of inaction can be deadly,” Alathari said.

title: New York congressional candidate Brad Lander says IDF detained him in the occupied West Bank
summary: Lander later said Israeli authorities released him after they detained him and dozens of other volunteers for harvesting olives near a settlement.
story: Congressional candidate Brad Lander said Wednesday that the Israel Defense Forces detained him in the occupied West Bank while he was participating in an olive harvest.
Lander, who is running in New York’s 10th District, said in an interview that he was later released with a warning.

Lander, a former New York City comptroller, said he was harvesting olives for Palestinians in the West Bank along with more than 40 international volunteers, including Americans, and 28 Israelis, who were affiliated with a coalition of human rights groups. Israeli authorities told him that his actions were illegal and that the group had been “causing a disturbance of public order,” he said.

“But I assure you, all we were doing was harvesting olives,” he said. “So if by ‘disturbance of public order’ they mean the order of the Israeli occupation of the West Bank, I guess maybe, but we were very peacefully harvesting olives.”

Beck Strober, a spokesperson for Protect the Harvest, one of the groups involved in the volunteer effort, told NBC News on Wednesday afternoon that all but four of those who were detained have been released. The Israeli members of the group will not be allowed to return to the West Bank for 28 days, Strober said.

Lander later said on X that everyone in the Protect the Harvest delegation has been released but that the multiweek ban for Israelis in the group “means they will be unable to participate in the olive harvest.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The IDF said in a statement that soldiers, border police and other officers detained people harvesting olives “due to the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community.”

“Harvesting in this area requires a request to be submitted to the relevant authorities in advance of the start of the olive harvest season,” the IDF said. “This coordination is necessary to ensure the security of the area and maintain public order.”
Lander told NBC News that he was apparently released from detention because of his “public profile,” adding that Israeli authorities kept calling him “congressman.”

“I tried to explain to them I wasn’t a member of Congress, just a primary winner,” he said, referring to the Democratic primary this year. “If they don’t want a diplomatic or international incident, they should stop state-sponsored ethnic cleansing. Releasing me is not going to change the facts of occupation.”

Lander’s 10th District primary race against Rep. Dan Goldman was dominated by the candidates’ views about Israel. Both men are Jewish, and Lander has been more critical of Israel’s government and the war in Gaza, which he has said is a “genocide.”

The olive grove in which the group was volunteering had not been harvested since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, according to Lander and the spokesperson for Protect the Harvest. Lander said Palestinian farmers “haven’t felt safe to harvest their olive trees” because of the grove’s proximity to a nearby Israeli settlement.

Last week brought high-profile Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians and others, including one in which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was injured and another that targeted European diplomats. Israeli police said this week that they arrested 10 people suspected of participating in the violence against Palestinians and others.

More than 900 Palestinians had been injured in settler attacks since the start of the year, a United Nations report said in July. The report said 76 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank were killed by Israeli forces or settlers or died from their injuries since the start of the year.

Lander and other volunteers were detained after about two hours of harvesting, when, Lander said, the group spotted what he believed to be a security car from an Israeli settlement watching them. Shortly afterward, a group of IDF soldiers and police officers arrived and asked the group for passports, he said. Eventually, the harvesters were loaded onto a bus and driven to a military station in the West Bank.
The group was not asked to leave before being detained, Lander said, adding that if Israeli authorities had asked, “we would have left.”
The CEO of T’ruah, a Jewish human rights group, and 11 other U.S. rabbis affiliated with it were among those detained, a communications firm for the organization said in a news release.

In a statement, T’ruah CEO Rabbi Jill Jacobs called the IDF’s actions “an outrageous abuse of power, and part of a systematic, state-backed campaign of ethnic cleansing aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.”
“We will not be intimidated into silence,” she said later in the statement.

Lander previously posted that he was visiting the occupied West Bank with Protect the Harvest, which he said was “bringing people together from around the world to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the face of state-sanctioned settler terrorism.”
“Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest — and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he said Monday on X.

Last year, Lander was detained with more than 70 other people, including about a dozen elected officials, as they tried to inspect the living conditions at an immigrant detention facility in New York City. He was found not guilty this year of misdemeanor charges related to the incident.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump policy restricting treatment for transgender inmates
summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said the Trump administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison.
story: WASHINGTON — In a blow to President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court on Wednesday said his administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison.

The justices in a brief order rejected an emergency application filed by the administration that sought to block a lower court injunction against the proposal. The court order included no explanation, saying only that two conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, would have granted it.
There are about 1,000 transgender inmates in federal custody.

“This is a critical ruling for our clients and all transgender people in Bureau of Prisons custody,” Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement.
“The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights,” she added.

The policy, which will continue to be litigated over in lower courts, is part of President Donald Trump’s broader effort to roll back moves to expand transgender rights. It was announced in line with his January 2025 executive order telling federal agencies not to acknowledge the concept of gender identity outside of the “immutable biological classification” of male or female.

“This order is a loss for common sense,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said in a statement. The administration will continue its efforts to “protect countless Americans from these dangerous, life-altering medical practices,” she added.

In several different announcements, the Bureau of Prisons over the last 18 months has said it will not provide gender transition surgery, hormone treatments or “social accommodations” such as wigs, padding or makeup.

That rolled back previous policies that allowed for gender-affirming care, with the government saying that such treatments have recently been called into question by medical professionals. That claim is heavily contested by transgender rights advocates.
If the policy had gone into effect, the only treatment transgender inmates would have been able to receive would be mental health services and potentially medications like antidepressants.

A group of transgender inmates sued, arguing the government had failed to adequately explain the change. They also alleged a violation of the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment, which bars cruel and unusual punishment.
The lead plaintiffs in the case, Alishea Kingdom, Jas Kapule and Solo Nichols, have all been receiving hormone treatment for several years.
For Subscribers

Washington-based U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the current policy in a ruling earlier this year, concluding that the Bureau of Prisons had failed to consider the merits of its past treatment of transgender inmates in formulating the plan.
For Subscribers

“Despite providing gender-affirming care to inmates in its custody for years, the government cites in the Program Statement zero evidence from its own medical or mental health professionals to support its conclusions,” he wrote. The government provided no evidence that the previous plan was “ineffective or harmful,” he added.
Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, also found that the proposal appeared to be engineered precisely to comply with the president’s executive order, concluding that the reasons given were pretextual.
In September, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected a Trump administration request seeking to block the judge’s final decision, with the panel split 2-1.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the lower court was guilty of “substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency” and was essentially faulting the Bureau of Prisons for following the president’s executive order.
ACLU lawyers said in court papers that the Bureau of Prisons has provided hormone therapy to inmates since 1992 while also gradually expanding access to other treatments and social accommodations.

The abrupt change without necessary explanation “gives rise to the inference that the agency’s purported reasons were not its actual reasons,” the lawyers wrote. “That glaring omission, as well as the unreasonableness of its decision, make it clear that the rationales were contrived to support the demand President Trump made” in the executive order.
The case marks a rare recent win for transgender advocates at the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority.

In June, the court upheld state bans on transgender athletes seeking to participate in women’s and girls’ sports. A year earlier, the court backed state laws banning gender transition treatments for transgender youths.
The court has also allowed Trump to implement a ban on transgender people in the military.

title: Vance says Republicans should ‘stop whining’ about Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad if they want to win
summary: Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother.
story: Vice President JD Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother.

“Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance told reporters on Wednesday in Cincinnati.

The Ohio Republican’s ad targeting his Acton exploded across the political landscape on Tuesday, sparking criticism from both sides of the aisle in the final stretch of the battleground gubernatorial race.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is running for a full term in the Senate after he was appointed to fill Vance’s former seat, said that he “would not have run that ad.”

Ramaswamy’s ad features Acton’s estranged mother calling her daughter a “liar” and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton previously recounted being sexually abused by her mother’s husband as a child, and Acton’s brother said on Tuesday that their “birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
Acton previously said in a 2019 interview with The Youngstown Vindicator that she had not seen her mother since a hearing in the 1978 court case against Acton’s stepfather.

Conservative commentator Meghan McCain said on X that the ad was “dastardly” and “never should have been created.” An aide for Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, deleted his post that shared the video. The aide, Dan Hauser, apologized and said he deleted his post “after researching it, and the disturbing allegations.”

Vance brushed off concerns about the ad, instead criticizing Republicans who condemned it. Speaking to reporters in Ohio on Wednesday, Vance said that “whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” adding that he was focused on who would win the elections.
Vance says GOP should 'stop whining' about Ramaswamy ad

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he said.
He also urged Republicans to “remember some of the ads that have been run against me” and other Republicans.
Vance brought up the ad in an Ohio rally Wednesday afternoon, though he said he “wasn’t even supposed to talk about” the controversy, “but I cannot help myself.”

“Now the media and the Democrats of the state of Ohio are obsessed, because guess what, Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”
“My message, ladies and gentlemen, is very simple: Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts,” he said, going on to criticize Acton.
Vance’s and Ramaswamy’s political circles have notable overlaps. NBC News previously reported that several members of Ramaswamy’s campaign previously worked on Vance’s political team.
Ramaswamy’s team is planning a $4 million statewide advertising push around the ad.
Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, responded to the ad on Tuesday, slamming Ramaswamy.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said.
Stearns said that he and his sister were removed from their mother and stepfather’s custody after their stepfather was arrested.
Attempts to reach Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, by phone and email on Tuesday were unsuccessful.

title: I’m a Therapist Trained to Read Facial Cues. This Is Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Is So Unsettling
summary: A psychologist reacts to You Can See Everything, why it’s such an unsettling experience and the body language of Elizabeth Holmes, Nathan Fielder and Billy Evans.
story: “Take it From Me” is a TODAY series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this edition, a licensed therapist with a degree in cognitive neuroscience weighs in on “You Can See Everything.”
Spoilers ahead for “You Can See Everything.”
If you walk into “You Can See Everything” expecting answers, you might come out of the theater with more questions.

And if you walk into “You Can See Everything” as a clinical psychologist who studies body language and facial cues, you immediately get another ticket. At least that was the case for Morgan Starr-Riestis, who, as of Oct. 20, saw the movie twice since its Oct. 16 release.
Starr-Riestis, a therapist who has a specific training in nervous system regulation, body language and facial cues, says the movie is an “unsettling” experience.

“We’ve learned to track each other’s facial expressions and micro expressions. To be honest, as somebody that’s trained in this, it was hard to read, especially the first half of it,” she tells TODAY.com.
The documentary, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, opens 34 days before Elizabeth Holmes surrenders to prison for four counts of fraud related to her work with Theranos.

Already attracting Oscar buzz (unexpected, considering a documentary has never been up for best picture), critics are calling it “a fascinatingly intimate portrait of a deluded or disingenuous scammer.”

Famous for becoming the world’s youngest female billionaire, Holmes was convicted by a jury in a California court of four federal charges of wire fraud for misrepresenting to investors what Theranos’ blood-testing Edison machines were actually capable of doing.

Fielder attempts to investigate whether Holmes knowingly defrauded investors — whether she intentionally lied. Holmes dodges the characterization, attesting she has never told a lie before, not even a white lie. Another telling moment involving a famous comedy sketch might indicate she doesn’t pick up on social cues.

But viewers are divided as to whether Holmes is as naive as she seems. And insiders are not convinced by Holmes’ feigning innocence. John Carreyrou, the former WSJ reporter who shattered Theranos’ image of a revolutionary blood-testing device through his reporting, is skeptical, as is whistleblower Tyler Shultz. Carreyrou called it a “great film,” but said there’s “no chance” Holmes was just “along for the ride” with Theranos. Shultz wrote in a review for Stat News, a health and science publication, that she’s “still lying.”

For psychologists, it’s no surprise the film leaves audiences twisted as to who to trust. Is it Fielder, who turns himself into a character? Is Holmes somehow under the sway of her fiancé, Billy Evans, with whom she shares two kids?

Starr-Riestis caveats that body language isn’t always an accurate read of how someone is feeling. “Some people who have trauma histories or grew up around an angry caregiver, for example, can actually be hyper-sensitive to micro expressions more than someone who didn’t because they learned from a young (age) a certain furrow of a brow might be dangerous,” she says.
Not everyone is good at picking up social cues, too. “There’s also a wide range of reasons why someone might not read facial expressions as well — autism as an example,” she says.
Still, with those caveats in mind, here’s what she found on both watches of “You Can See Everything,” all six hours of it.
The ‘Dissociative Gaze’
Starr-Riestis called Holmes’ wide, unblinking stare during conversations with Fielder an example of the “dissociative gaze.”

“When our eyelids are pulled back like that and we’re unblinking, that’s usually a sign of fear or overwhelm. When you pair it with a smile, the mismatch is naturally unsettling. Our nervous systems just register it as something off,” she says.
A ‘Socially Disorienting’ Conversation Style That ‘Leaves Us on Alert’
The conversation style between Fielder and Holmes is unusual enough for it to be notable. Fielder’s style is “socially disorienting,” she says.

“He lets pauses hang, keeps his delivery flat, and doesn’t smooth over awkward moments the way most instinctively do. Normally, those small social cues tell us how to feel, so without them we’re left to read every interaction raw,” she says.
On Holmes’ end, her “words, tone and expression often don’t seem to match: warm, caring content delivered with a steady, still, intense gaze.”
“When someone’s verbal and nonverbal signals don’t line up, our nervous system registers the mismatch before we can name it, and we go on alert,” she says.
Amanda Seyfried’s ‘Warmth’ Is a Contrast

For Starr-Riestis, the movie changed in the third act when Amanda Seyfried unexpectedly enters the scene. Seyfried played Holmes in the Hulu series “The Dropout.” She reprises the role in “You Can See Everything” and also interacts with Evans, Fielder and Holmes (via a prison phone call) directly.
“What was a refreshing change was having Amanda’s facial cues. She’s so easy to read. You can watch the way her eyebrows rustle when she’s disturbed,” Starr-Riestis says.
Seyfried’s “warmth” is “absent in both Nathan and Elizabeth,” Starr-Riestis says. “To have both him and Elizabeth in the same room, you’re void of a lot of the normal social cues.”
Billy Evans ‘Staring Off’ and ‘Leaving the Room’
Starr-Riestis paid attention to Evan’s movements in the movie.
Evans, who met Holmes before she was indicted, frequently clashed with Fielder in the name of trying to protect Holmes. But some — including Seyfried — say he was controlling.
“You could see him staring off a lot. It felt like he was really trying to keep his anger in,” she says.
She says it seemed like he was trying to “be on his best behavior,” but he “had a hard time hiding it.”
“He would need to leave at certain points or remove himself because it felt like he was just keeping it all bottled (in),” she says.
‘Not Enough Cues’ to Find Out What’s Real
The movie leaves viewers feeling like they don’t know who, or what, to trust.
“I don’t have enough cues to figure out what’s real in this situation,” Starr-Riestis says.
The movie points to an “uncomfortable truth” she says we need to live with: “Each of us are living in our subjective universes.”

“I see it as a Venn diagram. There is overlap in our experience to where we can agree on things and have some sort of shared truth,” she says. “But you can’t see into someone else’s brain and perspective and perception. We can only know a portion of the truth.”

title: She Was 6 When She Played Zuzu in ‘It’s a Wonderful Life.’ Now 86, She Weighs in on New Jimmy Stewart Biopic
summary: Karolyn Grimes, once the little girl in It’s a Wonderful Life, had feedback for KJ Apa after seeming him in the new Jimmy Stewart biopic.
story: Karolyn Grimes played the part of 6-year-old Zuzu Bailey alongside Jimmy Stewart’s George Bailey in the 1946 holiday classic “It’s a Wonderful Life,” so she has firsthand knowledge of what the iconic actor was like.
When actor KJ Apa was portraying the legendary Oscar winner in the new movie, “Jimmy,” he got some direct feedback about his performance from Grimes, 86, who makes an appearance in the film.

“It’s interesting because my first time meeting her on set, she looked at me and she goes, ‘Huh. You look nothing like Jimmy Stewart,’” Apa said on TODAY Oct. 21 while laughing. “I was like, ‘Ohhhh.’”
The “Riverdale” star won her over with his portrayal of Stewart’s time as a fighter pilot in World War II as well as a few of his famous acting roles.

“Then I saw her after she watched the movie and she came and she said some really, really kind words,” Apa said. “And to have her stamp of approval meant a lot. Her and (Stewart’s daughter) Kelly, those were the only two people I was like, ‘If they’re happy with it, I can walk away really happy.’”
A sweet moment between Apa and Grimes after she first saw the film was captured in a photo Apa shared on Instagram on Oct. 9.

“I was so moved to feel the love & legacy that Jimmy left behind,” Apa wrote. “His life and work has made such an impact on so many of us and I could feel it last night. I am honored and grateful to have the opportunity to embody a man who loved his country, his family and lead through service. Jimmy Stewart was a good man. A decent man who always strove to do the right thing especially when it wasn’t easy. A simple and powerful reminder for all of us.”

Apa said he worked closely with dialect coach Eliza Simpson to embody Stewart’s inimitable voice and was busy “soaking in every part of him.” Stewart’s daughter Kelly Stewart-Harcourt gave her seal of approval to the film, which hits theaters on Nov. 6.

“But I was thrilled because the problem with somebody playing Dad ... was that you don’t want to sit there and listen to a Jimmy Stewart impersonation for two hours,” Stewart-Harcourt told Entertainment Weekly. “And Dad has such a distinctive way of speaking. It’s hard not to do an impersonation, but KJ channels him and brings him to life without doing a Jimmy Stewart impersonation. So I don’t see how they could have found anybody better.”

“Nothing makes me happier than Jimmy’s daughter Kelly loving the movie,” Apa said on TODAY. “That was the most important thing to me. People who love Jimmy, there’s so many of them. I had no idea it was that extensive how far his movies have reached.”
Apa used Stewart-Harcourt as a resource to learn more about her famous father, who died in 1997 at 89 years old.
“She shared so many stories about her father,” Apa said. “It was really special to have her involved every step of the way so that we could tell an authentic story.”

title: An Emotional ‘DWTS’ Dedication Night Ends With Shocking News

The remaining 10 couples are performing routines honoring the special people and places in their lives during the Tuesday, Oct. 20 episode.

After last week’s elimination of fan favorites Guillermo Rodriguez and Witney Carson, the pairs will give it their all to make it another week. In a turn of events, eliminated pro Alan Bersten is filling in for Val Chmerkovskiy after being suspended for his reaction to Carrie Ann Inaba’s critique of his wife Jenna Johnson’s performance.
His absence was quickly mentioned at the top of the episode by co-host Alfonso Ribeiro, who noted, “As you can see Alan Bersten is with Jenna Dewan because Val is not with us this week.”
As the night kicked off, Ribeiro and Julianne Hough welcomed Kym Johnson as she joined Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough as a guest judge.
